stem: Child male with cryptorchidism, low lying epicanthal folds, nuchal skin, what is the ddx:
why_right: A boy with cryptorchidism, epicanthal folds (with low-set ears) and excess nuchal skin (webbed neck) has the Turner-like phenotype of Noonan syndrome. Unlike Turner, Noonan occurs in males with a normal karyotype; other features include short stature, hypertelorism and pulmonary valve stenosis.
why_wrong_block: A. Marfan syndrome causes a tall, thin habitus with arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis and aortic root dilation; it does not cause webbed neck or undescended testes.
key_concept:
Webbed neck: think Turner (girl, 45,X) or Noonan (either sex, normal karyotype).
  • Noonan: short stature, webbed neck, hypertelorism, low-set ears, ptosis, pulmonary stenosis, cryptorchidism
  • Turner: girl, short, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation, primary amenorrhea
  • Prader-Willi: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, undescended testes
  • Marfan: tall, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic dilation
exam_pearl: Turner features in a boy = Noonan; right heart (pulmonary stenosis) in Noonan vs left heart (coarctation) in Turner.

stem: Child with Fecal soiling
why_right: In a child (beyond infancy) with fecal soiling, the usual cause is functional (idiopathic) constipation with overflow incontinence: retained hard stool stretches the rectum, sensation fades and loose stool leaks around the impaction. Soiling is a hallmark of functional constipation and points away from an organic obstruction.
why_wrong_block: B. Hirschsprung disease presents from the neonatal period with delayed meconium (beyond 24 to 48 hours), distension, bilious vomiting and an empty rectum with a squirt sign; soiling is rare because the aganglionic segment keeps the rectum empty.
key_concept:
Soiling in a child = functional constipation with overflow until proven otherwise.
  • Functional: onset after toddler years or toilet training, stool withholding, large stools, soiling, impacted stool on DRE.
  • Hirschsprung: symptoms since birth, delayed meconium, FTT, empty tight rectum, squirt sign.
  • Hirschsprung workup: contrast enema first, rectal biopsy confirms (absent ganglion cells).
  • Treatment of functional: disimpaction, osmotic laxative, toilet routine, diet.
exam_pearl: Soiling + stool in rectum = functional; constipation since birth + empty rectum = Hirschsprung.

stem: A 7-month-old child presents with vomiting and jaundice, but no hepatosplenomegaly. The child was previously healthy and tolerated breastfeeding well. Symptoms began after the introduction of fruits and fruit juices. Urine sediment test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Symptoms began after the introduction of fruits and fruit juices
why_right: A previously healthy, breastfed infant who becomes ill with vomiting and jaundice only after fruits and fruit juices are introduced has hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency). Fructose 1 phosphate accumulates, causing vomiting, hypoglycemia and liver injury, and fructose appears in the urine as a reducing substance (the positive urine test).
why_wrong_block:
B. Galactosemia presents in the first days of life once milk feeds start, because breast milk contains lactose; an infant who tolerated breastfeeding well for months does not have it.
C. Gluten sensitivity (celiac disease) follows introduction of wheat cereals and causes chronic diarrhea, distension and failure to thrive, not acute vomiting with jaundice after fruit.
key_concept:
Match the trigger food to the enzyme defect.
  • Fruit, juice, sucrose, honey: hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B).
  • Breast or formula milk from the first days: galactosemia (GALT); E. coli sepsis, cataracts.
  • Wheat cereals: celiac disease; diarrhea, FTT.
  • Positive urine reducing substances: fructose or galactose in urine.
  • Treatment of HFI: remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol from the diet.
exam_pearl: Same picture starting with milk in the first week is galactosemia; starting at weaning with fruit is fructose intolerance.

stem: A child with a history of asthma presents for evaluation. His medical history is notable for atopic dermatitis. The patient has experienced recurrent episodes of wheezing and coughing, especially at night and with exposure to triggers. Which of the following provides objective evidence of asthma?
why_right: The question asks for objective evidence. Atopy, family history and night cough are all supportive history, but only spirometry gives an objective measure: reversible airflow obstruction, shown by an improvement in FEV1 of at least 12% after a bronchodilator, confirms asthma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atopic dermatitis is part of the atopic march and raises the probability of asthma, but it is a history finding, not objective proof.
C. A family history of asthma is a risk factor that supports the diagnosis; it is subjective history and does not demonstrate airway disease in this child.
D. Nighttime cough is a typical symptom of asthma (and of poor control), but symptoms are subjective and shared with other causes of chronic cough.
key_concept:
Asthma diagnosis = typical symptoms + objective variable airflow obstruction.
  • Spirometry: FEV1/FVC reduced (obstructive).
  • Reversibility: FEV1 or FVC rise ≥12% after bronchodilator.
  • Normal spirometry but high suspicion: methacholine challenge (FEV1 fall ≥20% = positive).
  • Peak flow variability is an alternative objective test.
  • History (atopy, family history, night symptoms) supports but never proves.
exam_pearl: "Objective evidence" in the lead in means a test result, not a history item.

stem: 18 months old boy, came to clinic for review. The child is always hungry, drinks 1 litter of milk daily and eats dirt. Poor solid food intake. On exam He is underweight & has pale conjunctiva. Which the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: An 18 month old drinking 1 litre of milk daily with poor solid intake, pica (eating dirt), underweight and pale conjunctiva has iron deficiency anemia until proven otherwise. The first investigation is a CBC with blood smear: it confirms anemia, shows microcytic hypochromic indices and the smear features, and directs any further iron studies.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lead screening is reasonable in a child with pica, and lead toxicity can coexist with iron deficiency, but the pallor and milk excess call first for confirming and characterising the anemia.
C. Ophthalmology consultation has no role; pale conjunctiva is a sign of anemia, not an eye disease.
D. Ferritin confirms low iron stores and is a useful second step, but on its own it does not show whether anemia is present or its severity; the CBC comes first.
key_concept:
Toddler + excess cow's milk + pica + pallor = iron deficiency anemia.
  • Cow's milk is iron poor, displaces solid food and can cause occult GI blood loss in children under 2.
  • First test: CBC with smear (low Hb, low MCV, hypochromia, often high platelets).
  • Then iron studies: low ferritin, high TIBC.
  • Pica: think iron deficiency and lead exposure.
  • Treatment: limit milk, oral ferrous sulfate, recheck response.
exam_pearl: Ferritin confirms the cause, but the CBC confirms the anemia; the lead in "most appropriate investigation" here wants the CBC first.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with history of increasing eye puffiness for 1 week especially in the morning. He has had flu-like illness 2 week ago. On examination, he looks well, not in distress and no lower limb edema. Eye, chest and abdomen exams are normal (see lab results). Blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, Heart rate 88 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Total Proteins 35 (56-80 g/L), Albumin 16 (36-52 g/L), Protein +4 (Absent). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 5 year old with morning periorbital puffiness, normal blood pressure, albumin 16 g/L, low total protein and proteinuria 4+ has nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and edema. In this age group the cause is usually minimal change disease, often following a viral illness.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nephritic syndrome (e.g. post-infectious GN) gives hematuria, hypertension, oliguria and only mild proteinuria; here BP is 100/70 and the albumin is profoundly low, which fits nephrotic.
C. Hereditary angioedema causes episodic non-pitting swelling of face, lips or airway with normal albumin and no proteinuria.
D. Protein losing enteropathy also causes hypoalbuminemia and edema, but protein is lost in the gut, so the urine is free of protein; 4+ proteinuria points to the kidney.
key_concept:
Nephrotic = proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema (+ hyperlipidemia).
  • Proteinuria in nephrotic range (>3.5 g/day adult; 3+ to 4+ dipstick).
  • Periorbital edema worst in the morning.
  • Nephritic: hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, oliguria.
  • Child 2 to 6 years: minimal change disease; steroids first, biopsy not routinely needed.
  • Low albumin without proteinuria: think gut loss or liver.
exam_pearl: A preceding viral illness is a trap toward post-infectious nephritis; normal BP and massive proteinuria keep it nephrotic.

stem: Father has SC trait with 2 brothers who have SCD. Married a woman her family without SCD and the woman didn't test yet. What is the risk for baby?
OptD: Low risk and nil if mother test negative
why_right: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: a child is affected only if both parents pass a sickle gene. The father is a carrier, and the mother comes from a family without SCD and is untested, so the baby's risk of disease is low, and becomes nil if her hemoglobin electrophoresis is normal (the child could at most be a carrier). The correct step is to test the mother.
why_wrong_block:
A. High risk applies when both partners are known carriers (1 in 4 risk of SCD per pregnancy); only the father is known to carry the gene here.
B. No risk cannot be stated until the mother is tested; an untested partner could still be a silent carrier.
C. Advising against having children is not appropriate counselling, and even for two carriers the role is to inform options, not to forbid pregnancy.
key_concept:
Autosomal recessive counselling depends on BOTH partners' carrier status.
  • Carrier × non carrier: 0% disease, 50% carriers.
  • Carrier × carrier: 25% disease, 50% carriers, 25% unaffected.
  • Untested partner: test with hemoglobin electrophoresis before counselling a risk.
  • Affected relatives (his brothers) do not change the risk if the partner is negative.
exam_pearl: Father's affected brothers are a distractor; the risk hinges on the mother's test.

stem: A 6-years old with noticed progressive jaundice and mild tremors with decreased school performance. On examination there is stigmata of few chronic liver injuries. See labs. Hb 7, Retics 6, Direct bilirubin 20, Total bilirubin 25. What is the gold standard for diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with progressive jaundice, tremor, declining school performance, signs of chronic liver disease and hemolytic anemia (Hb 7, reticulocytes 6) has Wilson disease. The lead in asks for the gold standard: liver biopsy with quantification of hepatic copper content is the definitive diagnostic test, since serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper can be equivocal.
why_wrong_block:
B. A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion (biliary atresia, cholecystitis) and does not diagnose a copper storage disease.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is for suspected leukemia or marrow failure; the high reticulocyte count here shows the marrow is responding to hemolysis.
D. 24 hour urine copper is the most practical screening and supportive test for Wilson disease, but it is not the gold standard; that is hepatic copper on liver biopsy.
key_concept:
Wilson disease: liver + neuro/psychiatric + Coombs negative hemolysis in a child or young adult.
  • Screening: low ceruloplasmin, high 24 h urine copper, slit lamp for Kayser Fleischer rings.
  • Gold standard: liver biopsy with hepatic copper quantification.
  • Genetic testing (ATP7B) confirms in family screening.
  • Treatment: chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc for maintenance.
exam_pearl: "Gold standard" = liver biopsy; "most appropriate investigation" (sister card) = 24 h urine copper.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2352 → D. 24h urine copper excretion. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 6-years old with noticed progressive jaundice and mild tremors with decreased school performance. On examination there is stigmata of few chronic liver injuries. See labs. Hb 7, Retics 6, Direct bilirubin 20, Total bilirubin 25. What is the Most appropriate Investigation?
why_right: Progressive jaundice, tremor, falling school performance, chronic liver stigmata and hemolysis (Hb 7, reticulocytes 6) in a 6 year old point to Wilson disease. The lead in asks for the most appropriate investigation, meaning the practical noninvasive test: 24 hour urinary copper excretion is high in Wilson disease and is used with serum ceruloplasmin and slit lamp exam to make the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver biopsy with hepatic copper is the gold standard, but it is invasive and reserved for when noninvasive tests are inconclusive; it is not the first appropriate test.
B. A HIDA scan evaluates biliary drainage (biliary atresia, cholecystitis) and has no role in copper storage disease.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is for leukemia or marrow failure; the raised reticulocytes show an active marrow responding to hemolysis.
key_concept:
Wilson disease workup ladder.
  • First: serum ceruloplasmin (low), 24 h urine copper (high), slit lamp for Kayser Fleischer rings.
  • Equivocal: liver biopsy with hepatic copper (gold standard).
  • Genetics: ATP7B mutation analysis.
  • Clues: hepatitis or cirrhosis + tremor or behaviour change + Coombs negative hemolysis.
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "gold standard" flips the answer to liver biopsy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2351 → A. Liver biopsy. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 2-year-old girl brought to Primary Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. She had history of drinking 3 glasses of cow's milk daily, very picky eater and refusing to eat meat. The mother gave history of similar presentation on 2 of her brother (see lab results). RBC 3 (4.8-7.1 x 10^12/L Newborn; 4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L Child), Hb 4 (165-195 g/L Newborn; 112-165 g/L Child), MCH 18 (28-33 pg/cell), MCV 62 (80-95 fl), Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %), Platelets count 480 (150-400 x 10^9/L), Ferritin 9 (20-200 g/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: drinking 3 glasses of cow's milk daily
why_right: This recall is keyed to sickle cell disease. The source's reasoning rests on the similar presentation in 2 brothers, a familial pattern that points to an inherited hemoglobinopathy (autosomal recessive, so siblings share it), and on reticulocytes 3%, above the printed range, suggesting increased red cell turnover. A suspected hemoglobinopathy in a pale child is confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Alpha thalassemia trait gives only a mild microcytic anemia with a normal or high RBC count and normal ferritin; Hb this low with ferritin 9 does not fit a trait.
C. Iron deficiency fits the cow's milk excess, refusal of meat, MCV 62, ferritin 9 and platelets 480, but this recall's key gives more weight to the two affected brothers, a familial pattern that a dietary cause does not explain.
D. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic inflammatory illness, none is described, and ferritin is normal or raised rather than 9.
key_concept:
Pale child with microcytic indices: sort nutrition, inheritance and inflammation.
  • Iron deficiency: excess cow's milk, poor meat intake, low ferritin, reactive thrombocytosis.
  • Sickle cell disease: chronic hemolytic anemia, raised reticulocytes, affected siblings (autosomal recessive).
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with normal ferritin and high RBC count.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: chronic illness, normal or high ferritin.
  • Suspected hemoglobinopathy: confirm with hemoglobin electrophoresis.
exam_pearl: Affected siblings are the clue this key rests on; check the answer concern on this card before the exam.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2354 → C. Iron deficiency anemia. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Page prints Answer: A for this version; the near identical recalls 2354 and 2355 are answered C (Iron deficiency anemia).

stem: A 2-year-old girl brought to Primary Clinic because the mother noticed she is pale. History of drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily and is a very picky eater. The mother gave history of similar presentation on 2 of her brother (see lab results). RBC 3 (4.8-7.1 x 10^12/L Newborn; 4.6-4.8 x 10^12/L Child), Hb 4 (165-195 g/L Newborn; 112-165 g/L Child), MCH 18 (28-33 pg/cell), MCV 62 (80-95 fl), Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %), Platelets count 480 (150-400 x 10^9/L), Ferritin 9 (20-200 ug/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily
why_right: A 2 year old drinking 3 pints of cow's milk daily and eating poorly, with MCV 62, MCH 18, ferritin 9 and platelets 480, has iron deficiency anemia. Cow's milk is iron poor, displaces iron rich food and can cause occult intestinal blood loss in toddlers; low ferritin is diagnostic and reactive thrombocytosis is typical.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sickle cell disease causes a normocytic hemolytic anemia with normal or high ferritin; the affected brothers are a distractor, and the diagnosis would need Hb electrophoresis, not a dietary history.
B. Alpha thalassemia trait is microcytic but gives only mild anemia with a relatively high RBC count and normal or high ferritin; ferritin 9 and Hb this low point to iron deficiency instead.
D. Anemia of chronic disease requires a chronic inflammatory illness and has normal or raised ferritin, usually with normocytic indices.
key_concept:
Low Hb + low MCV + low ferritin (+ high TIBC, high platelets) = iron deficiency anemia.
  • Risk: under 2 years with excess cow's milk, picky eating, no meat.
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with normal ferritin and high RBC count.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: normal or high ferritin.
  • Treatment: limit milk, oral ferrous sulfate, recheck response.
exam_pearl: Family history of anemia in siblings is a trap toward hemoglobinopathy; ferritin decides.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2353 → A. Sickle cell disease. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 2-Year-Old Girl Brought To Primary Clinic Because The Mother Noticed She Is Pale. She Had History Of Drinking excessive amounts Of Milk and refuse to eat and solid food, Very Picky Eater And Refusing To Eat Meat. The Mother Gave History Of Similar Presentation On 2 Of Her Brother. Lab Results: RBC: 3, Hb: 4, MCH: 18, MCV: 62, Reticulocyte: 3%, Platelets Count: 480, Ferritin: 9. Which Of The Following Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?
why_right: A toddler with excessive milk intake, refusal of solids and refusing meat has an iron poor diet, and cow's milk in young children also causes occult gut blood loss and reduces iron absorption. The labs confirm it: microcytosis (MCV 62), low MCH, ferritin 9 (low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency) and platelets 480 (reactive thrombocytosis). The low RBC count also fits IDA, since MCV/RBC (62/3) is well above 13.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sickle cell disease is a normocytic hemolytic anemia with clearly raised reticulocytes, jaundice and normal or high ferritin; it does not give MCV 62 with ferritin 9. The brothers' history is a distractor toward hemoglobinopathy.
B. Alpha thalassemia trait is microcytic but the anemia is mild, the RBC count is high and ferritin is normal; it would fit a well child with MCV low but Hb near normal and normal iron studies.
D. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic inflammatory illness and has normal or high ferritin; it is right when ferritin is normal or raised with low TIBC in a chronically ill child.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: ferritin decides first.
  • Low ferritin, high TIBC, high platelets = iron deficiency
  • Normal/high ferritin, high RBC, mild anemia = thalassemia trait
  • Normal/high ferritin, low TIBC, chronic illness = anemia of chronic disease
  • Mentzer (MCV/RBC): >13 favours IDA, <13 favours thalassemia
  • Toddler on lots of cow's milk = classic IDA risk
exam_pearl: Family history of anemia is the trap; ferritin 9 with a milk heavy, meat free diet still means iron deficiency.

stem: An 8-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Room by her mother after ingestion of large amount of acetaminophen tablets. According to the mother, she ingested full 2 packs, containing 20 tablets. 1 day ago after she had fight with her. On examination, she has right upper quadrant abdominal pain, with nausea and vomiting. Blood pressure 95/50 mmHg, Heart rate 135 /min, Respiratory rate 25 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Which phase of acetaminophen toxicity she is at?
why_right: The ingestion was 1 day ago and she now has right upper quadrant abdominal pain, which reflects hepatic injury. Phase 2 (roughly 24 to 72 hours) is when the early GI upset settles but RUQ pain and liver tenderness appear with rising transaminases. She has no jaundice, encephalopathy or anuria, so she has not reached phase 3.
why_wrong_block:
A. Phase 1 is the first 24 hours: only anorexia, nausea, vomiting and malaise with normal labs; RUQ pain marks the move into phase 2.
C. Phase 3 (about days 3 to 4) is fulminant hepatic failure: jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, anuria; none is described here.
D. Phase 4 (from about day 4 to 2 weeks) is either recovery with normalising labs or progression to multiorgan failure and death.
key_concept:
Paracetamol toxicity phases by time and liver signs.
  • Phase 1 (0 to 24 h): nausea, vomiting, malaise, normal labs
  • Phase 2 (24 to 72 h): RUQ pain, liver tenderness, rising AST/ALT
  • Phase 3 (72 to 96 h): jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, renal failure
  • Phase 4 (about day 4 to 2 weeks): recovery or death
  • Symptomatic or raised LFTs at any phase: give N acetylcysteine
exam_pearl: RUQ pain or tenderness = phase 2; add jaundice or confusion and it becomes phase 3.

stem: 10 Y/O Child with cystic fibrosis, and the parent is asking what the proper counseling for this patient is. Which of the following is most appropriate?
OptC: No Need to test until 18 years old
OptD: Random blood glucose every six months
why_right: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes develops from progressive pancreatic damage and is often silent early, with fasting glucose staying normal until late. Guidelines therefore recommend an annual oral glucose tolerance test starting at age 10 in all people with CF, which matches this 10 year old. The OGTT detects post load hyperglycemia that fasting or random glucose misses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fasting glucose is insensitive in CF because early CF related diabetes shows post prandial hyperglycemia with a normal fasting value; it is the usual screen in type 2 diabetes risk groups, not CF.
C. Waiting until 18 misses years of undetected diabetes; screening begins at age 10.
D. Random glucose is not a screening test; it only diagnoses diabetes when ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.
key_concept:
CF related diabetes screening = annual OGTT from age 10.
  • Cause: pancreatic islet destruction (insulin deficiency)
  • Early phase: normal fasting glucose, high 2 hour value
  • HbA1c alone is not reliable for screening in CF
  • Treatment of CF related diabetes: insulin
exam_pearl: In CF the fasting glucose looks normal long after diabetes has started, so only the OGTT catches it.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with a high, relapsing fever of 9-day duration associated with marked irritability. a non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen and erythematous hands and feet, and a maculopapular erythematous rash on the trunk and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: swollen and erythematous hands and feet
why_right: Fever for 9 days (more than 5) plus four principal features, non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen erythematous hands and feet and a polymorphous rash, meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease. Marked irritability out of proportion to the fever is also typical. The next steps are echocardiography for coronary aneurysms and IVIG with aspirin.
why_wrong_block:
A. EBV mononucleosis gives exudative pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes, not cracked lips with swollen red hands and feet.
C. Rubella is mild with low grade fever, a cephalocaudal rash and postauricular or suboccipital nodes lasting about 3 days, not 9 days of high fever.
D. Measles has cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal rash; it does not cause extremity swelling or cracked lips.
key_concept:
Kawasaki = fever ≥5 days + 4 of 5 features (CRASH).
  • Conjunctivitis: bilateral, non-purulent
  • Rash: polymorphous
  • Adenopathy: cervical, usually single node
  • Strawberry tongue / red cracked lips
  • Hands and feet: edema, erythema, later desquamation
  • Investigate with echo; treat with IVIG plus aspirin
exam_pearl: Non-purulent conjunctivitis plus hand and foot swelling separates Kawasaki from measles.

stem: A 7-year-old boy who has recently visited his grandfather's farm, now presents to you with diarrhea, miosis, vomiting, lacrimation, salivation, excessive urination, and a garlic odor in his mouth. Which of the following should be administered?
why_right: A child from a farm with diarrhea, urination, miosis, vomiting, lacrimation and salivation has the cholinergic (DUMBBELSS) toxidrome, and the garlic odor points to organophosphate pesticide poisoning. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so atropine is given to block the muscarinic effects (titrated to drying of secretions), with pralidoxime and decontamination.
why_wrong_block:
B. N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol overdose, which causes nausea and RUQ pain with liver injury, not a cholinergic picture.
C. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (drowsiness, normal pupils, little secretion); it is avoided in mixed overdoses because it can provoke seizures.
D. Sodium bicarbonate treats tricyclic antidepressant toxicity (wide QRS, arrhythmias) and salicylate poisoning; it has no role in cholinergic excess.
key_concept:
DUMBBELSS (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating) + farm exposure = organophosphate → atropine + pralidoxime.
  • Atropine: muscarinic effects, endpoint is dry chest secretions
  • Pralidoxime: reactivates acetylcholinesterase (nicotinic weakness)
  • Remove clothing and wash skin
  • Paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine; benzodiazepine → flumazenil; opioid → naloxone
  • TCA (wide QRS) → sodium bicarbonate
exam_pearl: Pinpoint pupils with wet secretions = organophosphate; pinpoint pupils with dry, slow breathing = opioid (naloxone).

stem: Child with a history of going to birthday party , developed fever and KOPLIK spots in the mouth and mucopapular rash in the trunk - what is the mood if transition
why_right: Fever with Koplik spots in the mouth and a maculopapular rash after a crowded birthday party is measles. Measles virus spreads by the airborne route: respiratory secretions are aerosolised by coughing and sneezing and the small particles stay suspended in room air, which is why it is one of the most contagious infections and spreads easily at gatherings.
why_wrong_block:
A. Contaminated surfaces (fomites) matter for organisms like norovirus, RSV or MRSA; they are not the main route for measles.
B. Contaminated food and drink is the faecal-oral route (hepatitis A, typhoid, enteric infections), not measles.
D. This option was not recalled in the source; any non-airborne route would not fit measles.
key_concept:
Measles = airborne spread; needs airborne isolation (negative-pressure room, N95).
  • Prodrome: 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) + fever
  • Koplik spots on buccal mucosa: pathognomonic, appear before the rash
  • Rash starts on face/behind ears and spreads downward
  • Airborne: measles, varicella, TB
exam_pearl: Koplik spots = measles = airborne, not droplet.

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with symptoms consistent with measles. Three of the child's siblings also have similar symptoms. What is the most likely mode of transmission of this infection?
why_right: Measles spreading to three siblings in one household shows how contagious it is. Measles is transmitted by the airborne route: tiny droplet nuclei from respiratory secretions remain suspended in air and can infect people sharing the same space, even after the patient has left the room. This is why measles requires airborne (not just droplet) isolation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Droplet spread (large particles, about 1 to 2 m range) fits influenza, mumps, rubella, pertussis and meningococcus; measles is classically airborne.
C. Fecal-oral spread fits hepatitis A and E, enteroviruses and rotavirus, not measles.
D. Bloodborne spread fits hepatitis B, C and HIV, which do not cause household outbreaks of a rash illness like this.
key_concept:
Isolation by route:
  • Airborne: measles, varicella (chickenpox, disseminated zoster), TB
  • Droplet: influenza, mumps, rubella, pertussis, meningococcus, most pneumonias
  • Contact: MRSA, C. difficile, scabies
  • Fecal-oral: hepatitis A/E, rotavirus
exam_pearl: Rubella is droplet, measles is airborne; do not mix the two rash viruses.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Printed as an unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 2387.

stem: A 14-year-old-boy presents for a routine paediatrics exam. There is no history of any major illness. Physical examination confirms an irregular pulse with no other abnormal findings (see image). Blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, Heart rate 80 /min, Respiratory rate 20 /min, Temperature 36.8° C, Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, Height 175 cm (> 90th percentile), Weight 45 kg (25th percentile). Which of the following is most likely prognosis?
why_right: An asymptomatic 14-year-old at a routine exam with an irregular pulse and otherwise normal vitals and examination most likely has sinus arrhythmia, where heart rate rises with inspiration and falls with expiration. It is a benign physiological finding in children and adolescents, so the expected prognosis is normal development with no treatment needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Syncopal episodes would be expected with a pathological arrhythmia (e.g. heart block, long QT); this boy has no history of illness or symptoms.
B. A pacemaker is for symptomatic bradyarrhythmias such as complete heart block, not for a benign respiratory variation of the pulse.
D. Myocardial dysfunction would come with symptoms or signs of heart failure or cardiomyopathy, which are absent here.
key_concept:
Irregular pulse in a well child: think sinus arrhythmia first.
  • Varies with breathing (faster on inspiration)
  • Normal vitals, growth and exam
  • ECG: normal P before every QRS, varying R-R interval
  • No treatment, normal prognosis
exam_pearl: Asymptomatic + normal exam + irregular pulse = physiological, reassure.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'C. Normal development (MG)'. Image referenced but not shown on page.

stem: A newborn infant weighing 2 kg (small for gestational age) is noted to have a depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, upward slanting palpebral fissures, and an elevated epicanthal fold. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A flat (depressed) nasal bridge, upward slanting palpebral fissures and epicanthal folds are the classic dysmorphic features of Down syndrome. When a newborn has features of a chromosomal syndrome, the appropriate next step is chromosomal analysis (karyotype), which confirms trisomy 21 and identifies translocation forms that matter for parental counselling.
why_wrong_block:
B. Metabolic screening fits a newborn who becomes unwell after feeding (lethargy, vomiting, acidosis, hypoglycaemia); dysmorphic facial features point to a chromosomal cause.
C. TORCH screening fits SGA plus microcephaly, cataracts, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae or chorioretinitis; the SGA weight alone does not explain this Down syndrome face.
D. A skeletal survey is for suspected skeletal dysplasia or non-accidental injury, not for Down syndrome features.
key_concept:
Dysmorphic newborn: suspect a syndrome, confirm with karyotype.
  • Down syndrome face: upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge, small ears, protruding tongue
  • Other: single palmar crease, sandal gap, hypotonia, Brushfield spots
  • After diagnosis: echocardiogram (AVSD), thyroid function, hearing and eye checks
exam_pearl: Facial dysmorphism points to genetics (karyotype); SGA with organ findings points to TORCH.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2235 → C. Congenital infection screening (TORCH). Confirm before the exam.

stem: 8 y.o child presents with recurrent chest pain, found in high status, joints are laxed, and fingers arachnodactyly. Which of the following is most appropriate to rule out life threatening causes?
why_right: Tall stature, joint laxity and arachnodactyly suggest Marfan syndrome. Its life-threatening cardiac problems are aortic root dilation, aortic dissection and mitral valve prolapse, so recurrent chest pain must be assessed with echocardiography, which measures the aortic root and shows the valves.
why_wrong_block:
A. ECG is useful for ischaemia or arrhythmia but cannot measure the aortic root or show dissection, the danger in Marfan syndrome.
B. MRI brain is irrelevant to chest pain; it would be for headache or neurological signs.
C. CT chest (CT angiography) is used for suspected acute dissection in an unstable patient, but echocardiography is the standard first test to look for aortic root disease in a child with Marfan features.
key_concept:
Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1, autosomal dominant):
  • Skeletal: tall, arachnodactyly, joint laxity, pectus deformity
  • Eye: ectopia lentis (upward), myopia
  • Heart: aortic root dilation/dissection, mitral valve prolapse
  • Screen and follow with echocardiography
exam_pearl: Marfan + chest pain = think aortic root; echo is the test.

stem: A 5-week-old infant is brought to the clinic with a 3-week history of intermittent vomiting. After vomiting, the infant becomes very hungry and wants to feed again. Physical examination shows no alterations apart from a 2.50 kg weight loss (see lab results). Test Results Normal Values: Sodium 147 (134-146 mol/L), Potassium 2.9 (3.5-5.1 mmol/L), Bicarbonate 32 (21-28 mmol/L), Chloride 89 (97-108 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: becomes very hungry and wants to feed again
why_right: A 5-week-old with recurrent vomiting who is hungry right after vomiting, with weight loss, and labs showing hypochloraemic (Cl 89), hypokalaemic (K 2.9) metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 32) has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Repeated loss of gastric acid (HCl) causes this electrolyte pattern, and the typical age is 2 to 8 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gastric volvulus presents acutely with severe retching, epigastric distension and inability to pass a nasogastric tube, not weeks of vomiting in a hungry, otherwise normal infant.
B. Cyclic vomiting syndrome affects older children with stereotyped episodes and well intervals; it does not produce this metabolic alkalosis in a 5-week-old.
D. Malrotation with volvulus causes bilious vomiting and is a surgical emergency with an unwell infant, not non-bilious vomiting with a hungry baby.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis:
  • Age 2 to 8 weeks, first-born males
  • Non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry after
  • Olive mass in the epigastrium/RUQ
  • Labs: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: ultrasound; correct fluids and electrolytes, then pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: Bilious vomiting = malrotation (emergency); non-bilious + hungry + alkalosis = pyloric stenosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'C. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (MG)'.

stem: A 6 years old was brought by his parents with history of sudden abrupt loss of environmental awareness with lip smacking followed by sudden return to normal baseline. Brain Imaging= Normal, EEG 3-Hz spikes. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: sudden abrupt loss of environmental awareness
why_right: A school-age child (6 years) with sudden brief loss of awareness, automatisms such as lip smacking, and an abrupt return to baseline with no post-ictal confusion has absence seizures. The 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG pattern with normal imaging confirms childhood absence epilepsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Complicated febrile seizure needs fever (age 6 months to 5 years) and is focal, prolonged (over 15 minutes) or recurs within 24 hours; there is no fever here.
C. Infantile spasms occur in infants (usually under 1 year) as flexor or extensor jerks with hypsarrhythmia on EEG, not 3-Hz spikes.
D. Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder with abnormal tone and delayed milestones, not episodic loss of awareness.
key_concept:
Absence seizure:
  • Age about 5 to 8, girls more than boys
  • Seconds-long staring, blinking or lip smacking, many times a day
  • No post-ictal phase
  • Triggered by hyperventilation
  • EEG: generalised 3-Hz spike and wave
  • Treatment: ethosuximide (or valproate)
exam_pearl: Abrupt return to normal with no confusion separates absence from focal seizure.

stem: Newborn with midline face deformity diagnosed with panhypopituitarism ( diagnosis is written) Thyroid low , Cortisol low , Growth Hormone low ( written no values ). What to do ?
why_right: In panhypopituitarism with low cortisol and low thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone must be started first. Thyroxine increases metabolism and cortisol clearance, so giving it before cortisol replacement can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Cortisol deficiency is also the immediate threat to life in a newborn (hypoglycaemia, shock).
why_wrong_block:
B. Thyroxine is needed, but only after glucocorticoid replacement has started; given first it can trigger adrenal crisis.
C. Growth hormone is needed, but it is not the urgent priority; untreated cortisol deficiency kills, GH deficiency does not in the short term.
D. Waiting a month is unsafe: the diagnosis is made and the newborn needs replacement now to avoid hypoglycaemia, adrenal crisis and brain damage from hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Order of hormone replacement in hypopituitarism:
  • 1st: glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone)
  • 2nd: thyroxine
  • Then: growth hormone, sex steroids at puberty
  • Midline facial defects (e.g. septo-optic dysplasia, cleft) are linked to pituitary deficiency
exam_pearl: Steroids before thyroid: never give thyroxine first when cortisol is low.

stem: A 4-Year-Old Child Presents With Shortness Of Breath And Cough Following Flu-Like Illness For 2 Days. Examination Reveals Child In Severe Distress With Increased Effort Of Respiration With Bilateral Wheeze And Prolonged Expiratory Phase. He Had Similar Attacks Before That Required Hospitalization. Blood Pressure: 100/65 mmHg, Heart Rate: 124 /min, Respiratory Rate: 33 /min, Temperature: 36.6 °C, Oxygen Saturation: 82 %. Which Of The Following Is The Most Appropriate Management?
highlight_terms_source: Bilateral Wheeze And Prolonged Expiratory Phase
why_right: A 4-year-old with prior attacks needing hospitalisation, now with bilateral wheeze, prolonged expiration, severe distress and SpO2 82% after a viral trigger, has an acute severe asthma exacerbation. The core treatment is an inhaled short-acting beta-agonist (Ventolin/salbutamol nebulisation) plus systemic corticosteroid, with oxygen to correct the hypoxaemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics are not indicated: the trigger is viral and the child is afebrile; and this option omits the bronchodilator, the most important drug.
B. Antibiotics add nothing in a viral asthma attack and the systemic steroid is missing; antibiotics are only for proven bacterial infection or pneumonia.
C. IV fluids are not part of standard asthma treatment unless the child is dehydrated, and this option omits the systemic steroid.
key_concept:
Acute asthma in children:
  • Oxygen to keep SpO2 about 94 to 98%
  • Salbutamol (nebuliser or spacer), repeated
  • Ipratropium added in severe attacks
  • Systemic steroid early (oral prednisolone or IV)
  • Not responding: IV magnesium, then ICU
  • Antibiotics only with clear bacterial infection
exam_pearl: Asthma attack = bronchodilator + steroid; antibiotics are the distractor.

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with new-onset exertional dyspnea and palpitations following a viral URI 3 weeks ago. Exam shows tachycardia, tachypnea, and gallop rhythm. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: New exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, tachycardia and a gallop rhythm appearing 3 weeks after a viral URI suggest viral myocarditis with heart failure (the chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly). Echocardiography is the most appropriate test because it shows ventricular dilation, reduced systolic function, wall motion abnormalities and effusion, and excludes structural heart disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. ECG is supportive (sinus tachycardia, low voltage, ST-T changes, arrhythmia) but nonspecific and cannot assess ventricular function.
C. Viral serology may identify the virus but does not confirm myocarditis or guide immediate management; the virus is often not found.
key_concept:
Viral myocarditis in children:
  • Follows a viral illness (enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, adenovirus)
  • Heart failure signs: tachycardia, tachypnoea, gallop, hepatomegaly
  • CXR: cardiomegaly
  • Echo: dilated poorly contracting ventricles; key first test
  • Cardiac MRI and endomyocardial biopsy confirm in selected cases
exam_pearl: Post-viral child with gallop and cardiomegaly = myocarditis; echo first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot with chest X-ray (cardiomegaly); answer line 'A- Echocardiography (confirmed)'.

stem: Pediatric patient age 2 days old post SVD presented to the ER with bleeding and hemarthrosis labs showed Prolonged PTT, Normal PT no family history of bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: An isolated prolonged PTT with a normal PT localises the defect to the intrinsic pathway (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII), and hemarthrosis is the hallmark bleed of hemophilia. Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) is the commonest of these. "No family history" does not exclude it, because a substantial proportion of cases arise from new mutations.
why_wrong_block:
B. ITP is a platelet problem: it causes petechiae, purpura and mucosal bleeding with a low platelet count and normal PT and PTT. Joint bleeding and an abnormal PTT do not fit.
C. The option text is incomplete in the recall. Syndromic platelet disorders give mucocutaneous bleeding with normal clotting times, so they do not explain an isolated prolonged PTT with hemarthrosis.
D. Liver disease reduces several factors, including factor VII, so the PT is prolonged early. A normal PT argues strongly against it, and it is not a cause of bleeding in a healthy 2-day-old.
key_concept:
Read the coagulation screen first, then the bleeding pattern.
  • Isolated PTT prolonged: VIII, IX, XI, XII (hemophilia A or B)
  • Isolated PT prolonged: factor VII
  • PT and PTT both prolonged: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, common pathway, DIC
  • Low platelets, normal PT/PTT: ITP
  • Joint and deep muscle bleeds = factor deficiency; petechiae and mucosal bleeds = platelet or von Willebrand problem
exam_pearl: Day 2 bleeding makes you think vitamin K deficiency, but that prolongs PT as well; a normal PT with long PTT points to hemophilia.

stem: A 6-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with a 10-hour history of feeling unwell and tired. On examination, she is pale, has a palpable liver, and her spleen is 6 cm below the costal margin. Vital signs: BP 93/55 mmHg, HR 169/min, RR 28/min, Temp 37.5°C. Lab results: Hb: 52 g/L (112–165); Platelets: 102 × 10⁹/L (150–400); Sickle cell screen: Positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: spleen is 6 cm below the costal margin
why_right: A sickle-positive child with an acutely enlarged spleen (6 cm below the costal margin), severe anemia (Hb 52) and shock physiology (HR 169, BP 93/55) over only 10 hours is splenic sequestration: blood pools rapidly in the spleen. The mild thrombocytopenia also reflects platelet trapping in the spleen. The large spleen with sudden pallor is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
B. Evans syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia plus immune thrombocytopenia (positive Coombs). It does not cause a massively enlarged spleen with hypovolemic shock in a sickle cell child.
C. Sepsis is a real risk in sickle cell (functional asplenia), but the temperature is only 37.5°C and sepsis would not explain an acutely enlarging spleen with a sharp Hb fall.
D. Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19) causes severe anemia with a very low reticulocyte count but no splenic enlargement; choose it when the child is pale with a normal sized spleen.
key_concept:
Sickle cell crisis: let the spleen and reticulocytes decide.
  • Sequestration: big spleen, falling Hb, shock, often low platelets; treat with urgent transfusion
  • Recurrent sequestration: splenectomy
  • Aplastic: parvovirus B19, low reticulocytes, no splenomegaly
  • Vaso-occlusive: pain (hands and feet in young children), Hb near baseline
  • Hemolytic: jaundice, high reticulocytes
exam_pearl: Pale sickle child plus a large spleen = sequestration; pale plus normal spleen with low reticulocytes = aplastic crisis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked A (MG).

stem: 8 years old girl brought to primary healthcare clinic by her mother, complaining of poor concentration and hyperactivity at school. Her teacher noticed that she has difficulty staying seated at her place. The mother reported that her daughter only sleeps 5 hours per night from 1 AM to 6 AM. What’s the most appropriate step in management?
OptD: Blood test to check for Anemia
highlight_terms_source: poor concentration and hyperactivity at school
only sleeps 5 hours per night from 1 AM to 6 AM
why_right: An 8-year-old sleeping only 5 hours (1 AM to 6 AM) is severely sleep deprived, and in children sleep deprivation commonly shows up as hyperactivity and poor concentration rather than sleepiness. The first, most appropriate step is to correct the cause with behavioural sleep measures: a fixed bedtime, a consistent wind-down routine and no screens before bed. Only if symptoms persist once sleep is adequate should ADHD be assessed formally.
why_wrong_block:
A. Melatonin is not first line; it is considered only after behavioural sleep measures fail, for example in persistent sleep onset problems or neurodevelopmental conditions.
B. Nothing in the history suggests a neurological disorder (no seizures, regression or focal signs); the obvious, reversible cause is the sleep pattern.
D. Iron deficiency can contribute to poor attention or restless sleep, but there is no pallor or other clue here; testing for anemia is not the most appropriate first step when inadequate sleep is clearly documented.
key_concept:
Inattention or hyperactivity in a child: exclude reversible causes before labelling ADHD.
  • Insufficient sleep or poor sleep hygiene: fix the routine first
  • Snoring, apneas: think obstructive sleep apnea (adenotonsillar hypertrophy)
  • Hearing or vision problems, learning difficulty, stress at home
  • ADHD diagnosis needs symptoms in two or more settings for at least 6 months
  • Treatment ladder for sleep problems: behavioural measures before melatonin
exam_pearl: A child who goes to bed at 1 AM is not 'hyperactive' until proven otherwise; sleep routine comes before pills or tests.

stem: Family brought their kid who has a fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested some seed. Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound. X ray pictures was shown. What is the next thing to do?
OptC: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
highlight_terms_source: hx of choking after he ingested some seed
why_right: A choking episode while eating seeds followed by reduced breath sounds on the right is foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise; the fever and cough suggest infection developing behind the obstruction. The next step is bronchoscopy (rigid, in children), which both confirms the diagnosis and removes the object. Antibiotics or symptomatic care will fail while the seed remains.
why_wrong_block:
A. Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension) or for severe croup in nebulised form; it does nothing for a mechanical obstruction in a bronchus.
C. Treating this as a simple viral URTI misses the foreign body and risks recurrent pneumonia, lung collapse or bronchiectasis. The choking history and one-sided signs mandate removal.
D. IV access, fluids or antibiotics may be part of supportive care, but they are not the definitive next step; the obstruction must be removed.
key_concept:
Witnessed choking + unilateral signs = bronchoscopy, even if the X-ray looks normal.
  • Most aspirated items in children are organic (seeds, nuts) and radiolucent
  • X-ray clues: unilateral hyperinflation from air trapping (expiratory film), atelectasis, or post-obstructive pneumonia
  • The right main bronchus is the commonest site (wider, more vertical)
  • Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic
  • Complete obstruction with distress: back blows or abdominal thrusts first
exam_pearl: Fever and cough after a choking episode is not 'just a cold'; recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe should also make you think of a retained foreign body.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question shown as a screenshot with a chest X-ray; 'Answer: B' printed in the screenshot.

stem: A healthy 7-year-old boy presents with short stature. He has normal growth velocity but delayed bone age. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Reassure the parents that the child will reach normal height by puberty
OptB: Order basic investigations (CBC, electrolytes, bone profile)
why_right: A healthy boy with normal growth velocity and delayed bone age has constitutional delay of growth and puberty. His growth is simply running late: puberty and the growth spurt come later than peers, and because the delayed bone age leaves more time to grow, he reaches a normal final height. Reassurance and follow-up of growth are the appropriate management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Screening bloods are chosen when growth velocity is slow, the child crosses centiles downward, or there are symptoms of systemic disease (malabsorption, renal, chronic illness). None are present here.
C. Sunlight is advice for vitamin D deficiency or rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, bone pain), which is not suggested in a healthy child growing at a normal rate.
D. Avoiding dairy has no role; it would reduce calcium and protein intake. Dairy restriction is only for proven cow's milk protein allergy.
key_concept:
Short stature: normal velocity = normal variant; slow velocity = look for pathology.
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, family history of late puberty, puberty late, normal final height
  • Familial short stature: bone age = chronological age, short parents, normal puberty, final height matches mid-parental target
  • Pathological (GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, chronic disease): falling velocity, often marked bone age delay
  • Turner syndrome in any short girl: karyotype
  • Mid-parental height best predicts final height
exam_pearl: Delayed bone age alone is not alarming; it is the growth velocity that tells you whether to investigate.

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by whooping sounds at the end of each episode. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by runny nose a few days ago. History revealed he did not receive his 2-month vaccine yet. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by whooping sounds
why_right: Paroxysmal cough ending in a whoop, perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting, preceded by a catarrhal phase (runny nose), in an infant who missed his 2-month vaccine, is pertussis. There is no conjunctivitis and no diarrhea to suggest Chlamydia or adenovirus. Young unvaccinated infants are the group most at risk of severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenovirus gives cough with fever, conjunctivitis and often diarrhea; choose it when those extra-respiratory features appear, which are absent here.
C. Mycoplasma pneumonia mainly affects school-age children and young adults, with a gradual dry cough and malaise; it is uncommon at 3 months and does not cause a whoop.
D. Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia has a staccato (not whooping) cough, preceding conjunctivitis, crackles, no fever and eosinophilia; the preceding illness here was a runny nose, not conjunctivitis.
key_concept:
Infant paroxysmal cough: the companion features decide.
  • Whoop + post-tussive vomiting, no conjunctivitis or diarrhea, unvaccinated: pertussis
  • Staccato cough + earlier conjunctivitis + crackles, no fever, eosinophilia: Chlamydia
  • Cough + conjunctivitis + fever + diarrhea: adenovirus
  • Pertussis: diagnose with nasopharyngeal PCR; treat patient and close contacts with a macrolide
  • Fever in pertussis suggests secondary pneumonia
exam_pearl: Missed vaccines + catarrhal start + whoop = pertussis; add conjunctivitis and diarrhea and it becomes adenovirus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked A (MG).

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of staccato cough, inspiration between each cough. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by conjunctivitis few days ago. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic with auscultatory crackles. He has normal white blood cell count with elevated eosinophils on laboratory evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The triad of a staccato cough, conjunctivitis a few days earlier and lower respiratory signs (tachypnea, crackles) in a young infant is Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia, acquired from the birth canal. The normal WBC with raised eosinophils is a classic supporting clue, and the absence of diarrhea argues against adenovirus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pertussis gives a whooping cough without conjunctivitis or crackles, usually after a runny nose rather than an eye infection; typical labs show lymphocytosis, not isolated eosinophilia.
B. Adenovirus also causes conjunctivitis and cough, but it brings fever and diarrhea; choose it when diarrhea is present.
C. Mycoplasma is a pneumonia of school-age children and adolescents and is not associated with neonatal conjunctivitis or eosinophilia.
key_concept:
Staccato cough + preceding conjunctivitis + afebrile pneumonia in an infant under 3 months = Chlamydia trachomatis.
  • Conjunctivitis typically appears around 2 weeks, pneumonia at about 4 to 12 weeks
  • Labs: normal WBC with eosinophilia
  • CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Treatment: oral macrolide (azithromycin or erythromycin)
  • Diarrhea present = adenovirus; whoop alone = pertussis
exam_pearl: Staccato cough with eosinophilia and a history of sticky eyes is Chlamydia, even if the paroxysms cause cyanosis and vomiting like pertussis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked D (MG).

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough associated with an inspiratory whoop and possessive emesis. It is associated with fever, conjunctival redness and diarrhea. His immunization is up to date. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Although the cough has an inspiratory whoop with post-tussive emesis, the accompanying fever, conjunctival redness and diarrhea point to a multisystem viral infection: adenovirus. The infant is also fully immunized, which makes pertussis less likely. Diarrhea is the key feature separating adenovirus from Chlamydia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pertussis causes isolated whooping paroxysms without fever, conjunctivitis or diarrhea, typically in an unvaccinated infant; a whoop alone is not enough when these extra features are present.
C. Mycoplasma pneumonia is a disease of older children and young adults and does not cause conjunctivitis with diarrhea in a 3-month-old.
D. Chlamydia also follows conjunctivitis, but it is afebrile, has a staccato cough and does not cause diarrhea.
key_concept:
Conjunctivitis + cough: check for fever and diarrhea.
  • Fever + diarrhea + conjunctivitis + cough: adenovirus (supportive care)
  • No fever, no diarrhea, staccato cough, eosinophilia: Chlamydia (macrolide)
  • Isolated whoop, no eye or gut signs, unvaccinated: pertussis (macrolide)
  • Adenovirus can also cause pharyngitis, gastroenteritis, croup, cystitis and pneumonia
exam_pearl: A whoop does not automatically mean pertussis; conjunctivitis plus diarrhea in a vaccinated infant means adenovirus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked B (MG).

stem: 5 year old child going for preschool vaccination, what is the most important prevaccination preassessment
why_right: The preschool booster at 5 years includes live vaccines such as MMR and varicella. Antibodies from a recent immunoglobulin or other antibody-containing blood product can neutralise these live viruses, so the dose may fail and must be deferred for a set interval. That is why this history is the key pre-vaccination check in this recall; inactivated vaccines are not affected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR or other routine childhood vaccines; it matters mainly for yellow fever vaccine, and current guidance gives influenza vaccine to egg-allergic children without special precautions.
C. Mild illness with or without fever is not a contraindication; only moderate to severe acute illness is a precaution that delays vaccination, so a fever check alone is less decisive.
D. Inspecting the previous vaccine site has no bearing on whether the next dose is safe or effective; a past mild local reaction is not a contraindication.
key_concept:
Pre-vaccination screening: true contraindications vs misconceptions.
  • Contraindication: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component
  • Live vaccines: avoid in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy; defer after immunoglobulin or blood products
  • Transfusion delays live vaccines only; inactivated vaccines are given on schedule
  • Precaution: moderate or severe acute illness
  • Not contraindications: mild illness, antibiotics, penicillin allergy, family history of vaccine reactions
exam_pearl: Recent immunoglobulin matters for live vaccines (MMR, varicella), not for killed ones; that is why it dominates the 5-year booster check.

stem: 4 months old with poor weight gain. At birth it was 3.3 kg, then became 4 kg. His mother uses 2 spoons of milk in 90 mL water, she feeds him every 3 hours. She's 19 years old, that's her first baby. What is the most likely cause of failure to thrive?
highlight_terms_source: 2 spoons of milk in 90 mL water
19 years old, that's her first baby
why_right: The infant has gained only 0.7 kg in 4 months (3.3 to 4 kg), far below the expected gain of roughly 25 to 30 g/day in early infancy. Feeding every 3 hours is an adequate frequency, so the problem is what is in the bottle: 2 spoons in 90 mL is over-diluted: most powdered formulas use 1 level scoop per 30 mL, so 90 mL needs 3 scoops, and each feed is short of calories. A young, first-time mother points to an error of inexperience in preparing formula.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neglect requires evidence such as missed feeds, poor hygiene, unexplained injuries or a disengaged caregiver; here the mother feeds regularly and the error is technical.
B. Celiac disease needs gluten exposure, which starts with weaning to cereals after about 6 months; it presents later with diarrhea, distension and buttock wasting, not in an exclusively formula-fed 4-month-old.
D. Feeding every 3 hours (about 8 feeds a day) is normal for this age, so frequency is not the problem.
key_concept:
Failure to thrive in an infant: start with the feeding history (volume, frequency, preparation).
  • Expected gain: about 25 to 30 g/day for 0 to 3 months, about 20 g/day for 3 to 6 months
  • Birth weight doubles by 5 months and triples by 1 year
  • Formula must be made with the scoop and water ratio on the tin; over-dilution gives poor gain, over-concentration risks hypernatremia
  • Downward crossing of centiles needs evaluation
  • Most infant FTT is non-organic (inadequate intake)
exam_pearl: Before suspecting disease or neglect, ask exactly how the formula is mixed; a wrong scoop count is the commonest fixable cause.

stem: Child diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome came to ER with abdominal pain and distention; mother said he vomit immediately everything he take. What could be?
why_right: A child with known nephrotic syndrome who develops abdominal pain, distension and vomiting has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proven otherwise. Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement plus ascitic fluid make these children prone to peritonitis, classically pneumococcal. The same scenario is keyed to peritonitis, the complication these children are at higher risk of.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pancreatitis: causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting, but nephrotic syndrome itself does not specifically predispose to it; consider it only if lipase is raised or the child is on drugs that cause it.
B. Hepatitis: presents with jaundice, RUQ tenderness and raised transaminases; nephrotic syndrome does not increase hepatitis risk and it would not explain acute distension with persistent vomiting.
D. Heart failure: gives edema, hepatomegaly and tachycardia with breathlessness, not an acute painful distended abdomen; the edema here is explained by hypoalbuminemia.
key_concept:
Nephrotic syndrome complications = infection + thrombosis.
  • Infection: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae), cellulitis
  • Cause: urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement, ascites as a culture medium
  • Thrombosis: hypercoagulable state (antithrombin III loss), renal vein thrombosis
  • Clue for SBP: abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, fever, rebound tenderness
exam_pearl: Nephrotic child + new abdominal pain and distension = think peritonitis first, not gastritis or hepatitis.

stem: 12-week-old child with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome with the mother concerned about increased risk for liver lesion. What tumor marker will you use?
OptD: Urine Homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
why_right: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome carries an increased risk of embryonal tumours, and the liver lesion the mother worries about is hepatoblastoma. Serum AFP is the tumour marker for hepatoblastoma and is used, together with abdominal ultrasound, to screen these infants in early childhood.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine oxalic level: used to look for hyperoxaluria in recurrent kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis, not a tumour marker.
C. PSA: a marker of prostate disease in adult men; it has no role in a 12-week-old infant or in liver tumours.
D. Urine HVA and VMA: catecholamine metabolites used for neuroblastoma (adrenal or paraspinal mass), not for a liver lesion.
key_concept:
Match the paediatric tumour to its marker.
  • Hepatoblastoma: AFP
  • Neuroblastoma: urine HVA and VMA
  • BWS screening: abdominal ultrasound (Wilms, hepatoblastoma) plus serum AFP (hepatoblastoma)
  • Wilms tumour: no blood marker; imaging
  • Interpret infant AFP against age norms, as it is physiologically high early in life
exam_pearl: BWS + liver = hepatoblastoma = AFP; BWS + kidney = Wilms = ultrasound.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AFP is used to screen for hepatoblastoma in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to the Paediatric Emergency Department in the early morning hours with a barking cough, that worsens with crying. There is a history of mild cough and temperatures around 38° C (rectal) over the last 3 days. Physical examination confirms an inflamed throat and mild suprasternal retractions. Blood pressure 95/65 mmHg, Heart rate 90 /min, Respiratory rate 34 /min, Temperature 39.3° C. Which of the following is the most likely at auscultatory finding?
highlight_terms_source: barking cough, that worsens with crying
why_right: A 3-year-old with a barking cough that worsens with crying, a few days of mild cough and fever, and suprasternal retractions has croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). The subglottic narrowing produces inspiratory stridor, which is the expected finding; the lung fields themselves are usually clear.
why_wrong_block:
A. Crepitation: crackles come from alveolar or small airway fluid, as in pneumonia or bronchiolitis; croup is an upper airway disease.
B. Wheezing: an expiratory sound of lower airway narrowing (asthma, bronchiolitis), not the inspiratory upper airway noise of croup.
D. Gasp: gasping is an agonal pattern of impending arrest, not the typical finding in a child with mild retractions and stable vitals.
key_concept:
Where the noise comes from tells you the level of obstruction.
  • Upper airway (croup, epiglottitis, foreign body in larynx): inspiratory stridor
  • Lower airway (asthma, bronchiolitis): expiratory wheeze
  • Alveoli (pneumonia): crackles
  • Croup: parainfluenza, barking cough, worse at night and with crying
  • Croup is a clinical diagnosis; treat with steroids, add nebulized epinephrine if distress
exam_pearl: Barking cough = croup = stridor; if the child drools and looks toxic, think epiglottitis instead.
