Gasping (no answer marked). Answer taken from the screenshot on the next page, where C. Stridor is marked with **.

stem: A 6-year-old boy complains of passing Coca-cola-coloured urine for the last week, with periorbital puffiness worse in the morning and fever. Congested throat and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy on exam. Which is the next best investigation?
why_right: Cola-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness worse in the morning and a recent congested throat with cervical lymphadenopathy point to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The first investigation is urinalysis, which confirms hematuria, RBC casts and proteinuria and so establishes a nephritic picture before further tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine culture: right when dysuria, frequency or a febrile child without another focus suggest UTI; here the fever fits the throat infection and the dark urine is glomerular hematuria, not infection.
B. Renal ultrasound: helpful for stones, obstruction or structural anomalies, but adds little in suspected acute glomerulonephritis.
C. Renal biopsy: reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases (persistent low C3, rapidly rising creatinine, nephrotic-range proteinuria), never the first step.
key_concept:
Suspected PSGN workup ladder.
  • 1st: urinalysis (hematuria, RBC casts, protein)
  • Then: serum creatinine for renal function
  • Best supporting test: low C3 with normal C4
  • Evidence of strep: ASO or anti-DNase B
  • Timing: about 1 to 2 weeks after pharyngitis, 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo
  • Management: supportive (fluid and salt restriction, treat hypertension)
exam_pearl: If the stem already shows RBCs in urine, the next test moves on to creatinine or C3, not urinalysis.

stem: A kid who won't move his lower limb presents with a swollen, hot, tender knee. What to do?
why_right: A child who won't move his lower limb with a swollen, hot, tender knee has septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Synovial fluid aspiration (cell count, Gram stain, culture) is the key step because it confirms the diagnosis and identifies the organism, and it should ideally be done before antibiotics are started.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood culture: a useful adjunct, but it is positive in only a minority and cannot confirm joint infection on its own.
C. IV antibiotics: essential and given promptly, right after joint fluid is obtained; giving them first can sterilise the aspirate and hide the organism. Right first only if aspiration would be delayed in an unstable or septic child.
key_concept:
Suspected septic arthritis: tap, then treat.
  • Clues: fever, refusal to move or bear weight, hot swollen joint, pain on passive movement
  • Key test: joint aspiration (synovial WBC very high, neutrophil predominant, Gram stain, culture)
  • Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Then: empirical IV antibiotics and surgical washout or drainage
  • X-ray is often normal early
exam_pearl: Asked for the most important test or what to do first: aspirate the joint; asked for treatment after the tap: IV antibiotics.

stem: A 7-year-old child presents with signs of meningitis. Laboratory investigations reveal a blood glucose level of 4.8 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows: Protein: 450 mg/dL (normal range: 150–450), Glucose: 3.8 mg/dL (normal range: 2.8–4.8), Predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of meningitis in this case?
why_right: The CSF shows a normal glucose (3.8, within its normal range and close to the blood level of 4.8), protein within the normal range, and a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Normal glucose plus normal protein plus lymphocytes is the viral meningitis pattern. The units in the recall are garbled, so read each value against the normal range given.
why_wrong_block:
B. Bacterial: gives a low CSF glucose, raised protein and neutrophil predominance with turbid fluid.
C. Tuberculous: also lymphocytic, but with low glucose and markedly raised protein, usually after weeks of fever and headache in an endemic setting.
key_concept:
Read CSF by glucose first, then cell type.
  • Bacterial: low glucose, high protein, neutrophils
  • Viral: normal glucose, normal or mildly raised protein, lymphocytes
  • TB: low glucose, high protein, lymphocytes
  • Fungal: similar to TB; think immunocompromise
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not mean viral: a low glucose with lymphocytes means TB.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents to the clinic for an annual physical assessment. The patient has normal growth and development and is able to do usual activities. His elder brother died due to a sudden cardiac death while walking to work. On physical examination, there is no cardiac murmur. Pulses are equal in all extremities. Which condition must be excluded before any sport is allowed?
highlight_terms_source: elder brother died due to a sudden cardiac death
why_right: An elder brother with sudden cardiac death in a young, otherwise well boy raises suspicion of an inherited cause, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young people. It is autosomal dominant and is often silent at rest, so a normal exam with no murmur does not exclude it; ECG and echocardiography are needed before sports clearance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bicuspid aortic valve: usually gives an ejection click or murmur and is not a typical familial cause of sudden death in youth.
B. Patent ductus arteriosus: produces a continuous machinery murmur (absent here) and is not a hereditary cause of sudden cardiac death.
C. Ventricular septal defect: produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border (absent here) and does not cause familial sudden death.
key_concept:
Family history of young sudden cardiac death: screen first-degree relatives.
  • HCM: autosomal dominant sarcomere disease, leading cause of SCD in young athletes
  • Murmur, if present, increases with Valsalva and standing
  • Screening: ECG and echocardiography
  • Others to consider: long QT, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary artery
exam_pearl: No murmur does not clear HCM; the obstruction murmur may appear only with Valsalva or exercise.

stem: A newborn develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Chest X-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures. What is the most important in management?
why_right: Respiratory distress shortly after birth with fluid in the interlobar fissures on chest X-ray is transient tachypnea of the newborn, caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and usually self-resolving. This recall's key is giving fluids, reasoning that a tachypneic newborn who cannot feed safely needs IV fluid support while the condition settles.
why_wrong_block:
A. NPO: withholding oral feeds while the baby is tachypneic reduces aspiration risk, but on its own it does not maintain hydration; this recall keys fluid support as the most important step.
B. Empirical antibiotics: right when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, worsening course); TTN itself is not infective.
key_concept:
TTN vs RDS in the newborn.
  • TTN: term, often C-section, fluid in fissures and perihilar streaks, resolves in 1 to 3 days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground glass (reticulogranular) X-ray
  • TTN care: supportive oxygen or CPAP, monitor, withhold oral feeds if tachypneic, IV fluids
  • RDS care: CPAP and surfactant, antenatal steroids for prevention
exam_pearl: Fissure fluid in a term C-section baby = TTN = supportive care, not surfactant or antibiotics.

stem: 9 years old child who had been bed weeting ,” his mother said he had POLYURIA AND POLYDIPSIA “ What is the firts invX :
why_right: New bed wetting in a 9-year-old together with polyuria and polydipsia is the classic way type 1 diabetes presents in childhood (osmotic diuresis). The first investigation is a quick random blood glucose; a value at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms is diagnostic, and ketones are then checked to exclude DKA.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine culture: right when enuresis comes with dysuria, frequency, fever or foul urine suggesting UTI; it does not explain polydipsia.
B. Behavioral changes: psychological causes fit secondary enuresis after stress without polyuria or polydipsia; organic causes must be excluded first.
key_concept:
Secondary enuresis + polyuria + polydipsia: rule out diabetes first.
  • DM: random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms
  • Then urine or blood ketones to exclude DKA
  • Diabetes insipidus: polyuria with dilute urine and normal glucose
  • UTI: dysuria, frequency, positive urinalysis
  • Psychological: diagnosis of exclusion
exam_pearl: A child who was dry and starts wetting again with thirst needs a glucose check that same day.

stem: Child i think he was 7yr came with ss of UTI asking about most diagnostic?
OptA: Mixed growth on clean mid stream urine
OptB: single growth colony × 105 of suprapubic urine
OptC: single growth of any colony of mid stream urine
OptD: single growth colony × 105 of bag urine
why_right: Urine culture is the gold standard for UTI, and suprapubic aspiration is the most accurate collection method because it samples bladder urine directly, bypassing urethral and perineal flora. A single organism grown from a suprapubic sample is therefore the most diagnostic result among these options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mixed growth on midstream urine: several organisms suggest contamination, not true infection; repeat the sample.
C. Single growth of any colony count on midstream urine: midstream samples need a significant count (about 100,000 CFU/mL) because low counts may be contaminants.
D. Bag urine: bag samples have very high contamination rates, so a positive bag culture cannot diagnose UTI; a negative one only helps exclude it.
key_concept:
Significant growth depends on how the urine was collected.
  • Suprapubic aspiration: any growth of a single organism is significant (most accurate)
  • Catheter: ≥50,000 CFU/mL
  • Clean catch midstream: ≥100,000 CFU/mL
  • Bag: not acceptable for culture
  • Mixed growth = contamination
exam_pearl: Any growth on suprapubic aspirate counts; a bag culture never confirms UTI.

stem: young boy had upper respiratory tract infection three weeks ago. Now, dyspnea on exertion, and on examination tachypnea, tachycardia, gallop rhythm, bilateral crackles on the chest, on X-ray bilateral opacities. Which if them is most helpful in confirming diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper respiratory tract infection three weeks ago
why_right: An URTI three weeks ago followed by exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, bilateral crackles and bilateral opacities points to post-viral myocarditis with heart failure. Of the listed findings, a gallop rhythm (S3) is the only one that is specific to ventricular dysfunction, so it best supports a cardiac (heart failure) cause rather than a primary lung infection. In practice the diagnosis is confirmed with echocardiography (plus ECG and troponin), which is not offered here; cardiac MRI or biopsy are the definitive tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tachycardia is nonspecific: fever, pain, pneumonia or anxiety all cause it. It supports illness but cannot point to the heart.
B. Tachypnea occurs equally in pneumonia, bronchiolitis or heart failure, so it does not distinguish a cardiac cause.
C. The history of a recent viral illness raises suspicion of myocarditis but is common and nonspecific; it suggests the diagnosis rather than confirming it.
key_concept:
Post-viral myocarditis: URTI then weeks later heart failure signs; the specific bedside clue is a gallop (S3).
  • Gallop rhythm = ventricular dysfunction / volume overload
  • Crackles + bilateral opacities = pulmonary edema, easily mistaken for pneumonia
  • Tachycardia and tachypnea = nonspecific
  • Confirmatory test: echocardiography (ventricular function)
  • Supportive tests: ECG, chest X-ray, troponin
exam_pearl: A child labelled "pneumonia" who has a gallop, tachycardia out of proportion and an enlarged heart shadow has myocarditis until proven otherwise.

stem: Which of the following cerebral palsy types is associated with Kernicterus?
why_right: In kernicterus, unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia (especially the globus pallidus). Basal ganglia injury produces dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy, with involuntary choreoathetoid movements. Its other classic cause is hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, and it is often associated with severe disability.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spastic CP reflects upper motor neuron injury (cortex or periventricular white matter), classically linked to prematurity and periventricular leukomalacia, not bilirubin injury.
B. Ataxic CP comes from cerebellar damage; it is not the pattern produced by basal ganglia bilirubin deposition.
C. Hypotonic CP is a nonspecific early picture that often evolves into another type; it is not the classic kernicterus association.
key_concept:
Match the CP type to the damaged site.
  • Spastic: pyramidal tract / periventricular white matter (prematurity)
  • Dyskinetic (athetoid): basal ganglia (kernicterus, HIE)
  • Ataxic: cerebellum
  • Spastic diplegia: legs much worse than arms
  • Spastic hemiplegia: one side of the body
exam_pearl: Kernicterus to basal ganglia to dyskinetic CP; prematurity points to spastic diplegia instead.

stem: A 12 months baby presented by his parents for check up, found that he didn't receive any vaccines except at birth vaccine. Normal development. Parents reported that he has recurrent URTIs and because of that they delayed the vaccinations until become healthy completely. What is the next step in management?
OptA: Refer the parents to social worker
OptB: Do blood test and immune test for baby
OptC: Reassurance and catch up all vaccines
OptD: Told them that the delaying in vaccines is the cause of recurrent infxs
why_right: This is a well, normally developing 12-month-old whose only problem is missed vaccines because of a misconception. Recurrent URTIs are common in young children, and a mild illness is not a reason to delay vaccination. The correct step is to reassure the parents and catch up all missed doses now; the series is never restarted, just continued with minimum intervals respected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Social work referral fits suspected neglect or refusal despite counselling. These parents delayed out of a misunderstanding and came for a check up, so education is enough.
B. Immune testing is for red flags such as severe, deep or opportunistic infections, failure to thrive or a family history of immunodeficiency. Simple URTIs with normal development are not an indication.
D. This is factually wrong: routine vaccines do not prevent common viral colds, so the delay did not cause the URTIs. Blaming the parents also does not solve the problem.
key_concept:
Missed vaccines in a well child: catch up now, do not restart.
  • Minor illness (URTI, low fever) is not a contraindication
  • Give all due doses at the same visit, respecting minimum intervals
  • Correct parental misconceptions with reassurance
  • Investigate immunity only with red flags (FTT, severe or opportunistic infections, family history)
exam_pearl: Recurrent simple colds in a thriving infant are normal and never a reason to hold vaccines.

stem: 3 months or years old not vaccinated I think 4 vaccines I remember MMR and OPV, what to do?
OptA: Reassuring and tell the parents it's unnecessary
OptB: Try to catch up missed vaccines
why_right: The recall describes a young child who has missed several vaccines (including MMR and OPV). The rule is to catch up the missed doses as soon as possible: the schedule is continued from where it stopped, never restarted and never abandoned, with minimum intervals between doses respected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Telling parents vaccines are unnecessary is wrong; an unvaccinated child remains at risk of measles, polio and other preventable diseases.
C. Waiting until school entry leaves the child unprotected for years; catch-up should happen at the current visit.
D. The text of this option was not recalled, so it cannot be judged; the catch-up principle still makes B the answer.
key_concept:
Missed vaccines: give them now and continue the schedule.
  • Never restart a series because of a delay
  • Several vaccines can be given at the same visit
  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) need age 12 months or more
  • Respect minimum intervals between doses of the same antigen
exam_pearl: Delay is never fixed by more delay; the answer to any missed vaccine question is catch up now.

stem: Baby 6 months with UTI, the parents were inquiring about the need for further investigation. What INITIAL investigation is required?
why_right: After a first febrile UTI in an infant, the initial imaging is a renal and bladder ultrasound to look for congenital anomalies such as hydronephrosis or obstruction. It is noninvasive, needs no catheter and no radiation, and its result decides whether further imaging is needed.
why_wrong_block: A. MCUG is invasive (catheterisation, radiation) and is not routine after a first UTI. It is indicated when the ultrasound is abnormal (hydronephrosis, scarring, suspected high grade VUR or obstruction) or after a recurrent febrile UTI.
key_concept:
Infant UTI imaging ladder: ultrasound first, MCUG only if indicated.
  • First febrile UTI: renal and bladder ultrasound
  • Abnormal ultrasound or recurrent febrile UTI: MCUG (looks for VUR, posterior urethral valves)
  • DMSA scan: renal scarring
  • Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first UTI
exam_pearl: "Initial" investigation = ultrasound; MCUG becomes the answer only when the stem gives an abnormal ultrasound or a second UTI.

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and absent secondary sexual characteristics. Her karyotype is 45,X. What is the most appropriate treatment at this time?
why_right: The 45,X karyotype with short stature and absent puberty is Turner syndrome, where short stature is caused by SHOX haploinsufficiency, not GH deficiency. This recall's key is growth hormone because the classic teaching is to maximise height first while the epiphyses are open, since estrogen accelerates epiphyseal fusion and ends growth. Estrogen is then added to induce puberty.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral contraceptive pills: not used to start puberty; induction uses low-dose estrogen increased gradually, and combined pills come later only for maintenance.
C. Estrogen therapy: needed in Turner syndrome to induce breasts and menses, so it is part of her care; the key ranks it after GH because early full-dose estrogen closes the growth plates and limits final height.
D. Gonadotropin replacement therapy: useless here because the problem is primary ovarian failure (streak gonads) with high FSH and LH; gonadotropins are for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
key_concept:
Turner syndrome treatment: height first, then puberty.
  • Diagnosis: karyotype 45,X (mosaicism possible)
  • Short stature: GH therapy while epiphyses are open
  • Ovarian failure: low-dose estrogen to induce puberty, progestin added later for cycles
  • Gonadotropins are not useful: FSH and LH are already high
  • Screen heart (coarctation, bicuspid valve) and kidneys (horseshoe kidney)
exam_pearl: In Turner syndrome the ovaries, not the pituitary, have failed: never give gonadotropins.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2224).

stem: Parents of a patient known case of epilepsy, they were inquiring about what to do for a seizure that lasts more than 5 minutes. What are they supposed to do until arrival of emergency care?
highlight_terms_source: seizure that lasts more than 5 minutes
key_concept:
Seizure of 5 minutes or more = treat as status epilepticus.
  • All seizures: safe environment, recovery position, nothing in the mouth, time it
  • 5 minutes or more: rescue benzodiazepine (rectal diazepam, buccal or intranasal midazolam) and call emergency services
  • In hospital: IV lorazepam (or IM midazolam if no access)
  • Persisting: second line IV agent (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, phenobarbital)
  • Never oral medication during a seizure
exam_pearl: The 5 minute threshold is the trigger to stop waiting and give the rescue benzodiazepine.

stem: Dehydrated with very low BP 50 something.
why_right: A dehydrated child with very low blood pressure has crossed from dehydration into hypovolemic shock. Children maintain blood pressure by tachycardia and vasoconstriction until late, so hypotension marks decompensated shock regardless of how the dehydration is graded. It demands immediate isotonic fluid boluses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mild dehydration has normal pulse, normal blood pressure and normal urine output; hypotension rules it out.
B. Moderate dehydration gives sunken eyes, dry tongue, rapid pulse and slow skin pinch, but blood pressure is preserved.
C. Severe dehydration (drowsy, weak thready pulse, very slow skin pinch, scanty urine) is the step before; once the blood pressure itself falls, the state is named shock.
key_concept:
Grade dehydration by clinical signs; hypotension means shock.
  • Mild: thirsty, normal vitals and urine
  • Moderate: sunken eyes, dry tongue, rapid pulse, slow skin pinch
  • Severe: drowsy, weak thready pulse, very slow skin pinch, scanty urine
  • Hypotension: decompensated hypovolemic shock
  • Shock management: 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, reassess, repeat
exam_pearl: In children hypotension is a late sign: a low blood pressure means decompensated shock, not just severe dehydration.

stem: Pediatric treated as pneumonia, received antibiotics, came back to ER with worse symptoms?
highlight_terms_source: came back to ER with worse symptoms
key_concept:
Pneumonia not improving on antibiotics: think complication first.
  • Parapneumonic effusion or empyema: dullness, reduced breath sounds, fluid on X-ray or ultrasound
  • Necrotizing pneumonia or lung abscess: cavitation on imaging
  • Resistant or atypical organism, or wrong diagnosis (foreign body, TB)
  • ARDS: severe hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates
exam_pearl: Failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics is the cue to image for effusion or empyema, not just to switch drugs.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 7-year-old patient presents with abnormal jerky movements, sore throat, and fever. His brother and sister had similar symptoms with fever. What is the most appropriate action?
OptA: Treat fever and reassure the parents
OptC: Perform throat culture and start penicillin
OptD: Obtain brain imaging and lumbar puncture
key_concept:
Fever plus abnormal movements in a child: first separate benign rigors from CNS infection and from post-streptococcal disease.
  • Rigors: conscious, stops with antipyretic, normal neuro exam
  • Meningitis or sepsis: neck stiffness, drowsiness, rash; give IV antibiotics
  • Encephalitis: seizures, confusion, focal signs; imaging and LP
  • Sydenham chorea: weeks after strep throat, irregular purposeless movements, emotional lability
  • GAS pharyngitis: confirm by rapid test or throat culture before antibiotics
exam_pearl: Sydenham chorea appears weeks after the sore throat, often without fever; chorea during an acute febrile sore throat should prompt you to rule out CNS infection.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Child came to ER before 12 hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphagia. On exam he looks toxic, immobile in a chair, opens his mouth with drooling of saliva, tachycardic, tachypneic and fever 40. Oxygen sat 88%. What's the next step?
highlight_terms_source: immobile in a chair, opens his mouth with drooling of saliva
key_concept:
Epiglottitis = airway first, then sepsis workup and antibiotics.
  • Picture: high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod or immobile, muffled voice, no barking cough.
  • Clinical diagnosis: do not examine the throat or upset the child.
  • Secure airway in a controlled setting (ICU or OR) by the most skilled operator.
  • Then blood culture plus IV 3rd generation cephalosporin.
  • Croup: barking cough, stridor, well looking; treat with steroids plus nebulized epinephrine.
exam_pearl: Drooling plus toxic look plus no barking cough means epiglottitis, so the answer is about securing the airway, never steroids or the ward.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Child with difficulty swallowing and congested throat, febrile, no cough, she is ill and sitting silently in her mother's lap but with her neck extended?
key_concept:
Epiglottitis sequence: keep the child calm, secure the airway, then culture and antibiotics.
  • Clues: toxic, drooling, dysphagia, no cough, tripod or sniffing (neck extended) posture.
  • Step 1: controlled intubation (OR or ICU).
  • Step 2: blood culture plus IV 3rd generation cephalosporin.
  • Croup instead: barking cough, stridor, nontoxic; steroids plus nebulized epinephrine.
exam_pearl: If the lead in asks for the antibiotic, ceftriaxone; if it asks what to do first, the airway.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 5-year-old child presents to the Emergency Room with severe sore throat, high fever and increasing difficulty breathing over 8 hours. On examination, ill toxic looking child with drooling of saliva and sitting immobile with open mouth. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 115/min, respiratory rate 32/min, temperature 38.8 °C, oxygen saturation 95%. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action should be taken?
OptA: Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy
OptB: Complete sepsis work up, followed by antibiotics for 7 days
OptC: Send home on oral antibiotics for 7 days and referral to ENT
OptD: Urgent admission to ICU for intubation then sepsis work to follow
highlight_terms_source: ill toxic looking child with drooling of saliva
why_right: Severe sore throat, high fever and difficulty breathing developing over 8 hours in a toxic child who is drooling and sitting immobile with open mouth is acute epiglottitis. The lead in is the immediate action: the risk is sudden complete airway closure, so the airway is secured first (ICU admission for intubation) and the sepsis workup and antibiotics follow. The normal saturation (95%) does not make the airway safe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy: tonsillectomy is elective treatment for recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea, not an emergency airway measure.
B. Complete sepsis work up, followed by antibiotics for 7 days: cultures and antibiotics are needed, but only after the airway is secured; doing them first can provoke obstruction.
C. Send home on oral antibiotics for 7 days and referral to ENT: suits a well child with simple bacterial pharyngitis; a toxic, drooling child must never be discharged.
key_concept:
Epiglottitis: airway first, then sepsis workup and IV antibiotics.
  • Picture: rapid onset over hours, high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod or open mouth posture.
  • Clinical diagnosis; avoid throat examination or distress.
  • Secure airway in ICU or OR.
  • Then blood culture plus 3rd generation cephalosporin.
exam_pearl: Any option that delays securing the airway (workup, imaging, throat swab) is wrong as the immediate action in epiglottitis.

stem: 10-year-old child presented to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and deep breathing. Laboratory results: Random blood glucose: 380 mg/dL; ABG: pH = 7.0, HCO3- = 10 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Glucose 380 mg/dL, "pH = 7.0", "HCO3- = 10", vomiting and deep breathing define severe DKA. The "most appropriate initial management" is IV fluid resuscitation followed by a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, which corrects dehydration, lowers glucose and stops ketogenesis.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is not routine and in children is linked to cerebral edema and hypokalemia. It is considered only in extreme acidosis (pH below about 6.9) or life-threatening hyperkalemia.
C. Subcutaneous insulin with oral hydration suits only mild DKA in an alert child who tolerates fluids. With pH 7.0 and vomiting, absorption and oral intake are unreliable.
D. Raising bicarbonate does not stop ketosis; only insulin switches off ketone production. This option misunderstands the pathophysiology.
key_concept:
Severe DKA (pH <7.1 or HCO3 <5): IV fluids then IV insulin infusion.
  • Diagnosis: glucose ≥200 mg/dL, pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 (ISPAD 2022: <18), ketones
  • Fluids first, then regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h; confirm K is not low before insulin
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls; continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • No routine bicarbonate
  • Main pediatric risk: cerebral edema
exam_pearl: Bicarbonate is the classic distractor in DKA: insulin, not alkali, clears ketoacidosis.

stem: A previously healthy 11-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of vomiting and diarrhea. His mother reports decreased oral intake and increasing lethargy over the past 12 hours. On examination, he is drowsy but arousable, and his breath has a fruity (nail polish-like) odor. Vital signs reveal mild hypotension. Laboratory results show: Random blood sugar (RBS): 8.9 mmol/L, Serum sodium: 131 mmol/L, Bicarbonate: 15 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of his current condition?
why_right: This recall's key is DKA because the child has vomiting, lethargy, hypotension (dehydration), a fruity (nail polish like) breath from acetone and a low bicarbonate of 15, the ketotic acidosis picture. Among the options DKA is the only diagnosis that accounts for ketones plus metabolic acidosis; the other options name a single lab finding or a non ketotic state.
why_wrong_block:
B. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia: describes a glucose number, not the cause of the acidosis and fruity breath; and RBS 8.9 mmol/L is not markedly high.
C. Hyponatremia: sodium 131 is a mild consequence of vomiting and diarrhea, not the cause of drowsiness and ketotic breath.
D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: needs very high glucose and high osmolality with little or no ketosis; here glucose is near normal and the breath is ketotic.
key_concept:
DKA needs hyperglycemia + acidosis + ketosis.
  • Clinical: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, lethargy, fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing.
  • Labs (ISPAD 2022): pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 18, ketonemia or ketonuria, glucose > 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL).
  • HHS: very high glucose and osmolality, minimal ketones.
  • Ketosis with normal glucose after poor intake: starvation ketosis.
exam_pearl: Fruity breath means ketones; check the glucose before calling it DKA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant listed under 2536 (Q: block).

stem: 5 months old child admitted to hospital many times with pneumonia. Came now with cough and monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing. What is the diagnosis test?
why_right: A 5 month old with recurrent pneumonia and a monophasic (single pitch, fixed) expiratory wheeze suggests a fixed central airway problem (tracheomalacia, airway compression such as a vascular ring, aspirated foreign body or congenital lesion) rather than asthma or bronchiolitis. The lead in is the diagnostic test, and flexible bronchoscopy directly visualizes the airway, shows dynamic collapse or obstruction, and allows lavage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest x ray: useful to confirm each pneumonia episode, but it cannot show dynamic airway collapse or the cause of a fixed central obstruction.
B. CBC and blood culture: assess infection or sepsis in an acute episode, but do not explain why pneumonia keeps recurring with a fixed wheeze.
C. Spirometry: the diagnostic test for asthma or COPD in older children and adults; it needs cooperation and is not feasible at 5 months.
key_concept:
Wheeze type points to the site.
  • Polyphonic, variable wheeze: small airway disease (asthma, bronchiolitis).
  • Monophasic, fixed wheeze: central or focal obstruction.
  • Recurrent pneumonia in infancy: think structural, aspiration, foreign body, immune.
  • Tracheomalacia diagnosis: bronchoscopy; laryngomalacia: laryngoscopy.
exam_pearl: Infant + recurrent pneumonia + monophasic wheeze means look inside the airway: bronchoscopy, not spirometry.

stem: Teenage girl sits on her ipad a lot and keeps comparing herself with others, she has low self esteem and anxiety, what’s the most she could benefit from?
OptB: Force her to leave social media
why_right: The teenager has low self esteem, anxiety and keeps comparing herself with others on her iPad: the problem is a pattern of negative thoughts, not severe depression. Cognitive behavioral therapy targets exactly these distorted comparisons and beliefs, and psychological therapy is first line for mild to moderate anxiety and low mood in adolescents.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antidepressant: kept for moderate to severe depression or anxiety, or when psychological therapy fails or is unavailable; not first for low self esteem with mild anxiety.
B. Force her to leave social media: coercive, damages rapport and does not address her thinking pattern; it is likely to be refused or resented.
C. Limit social media time: reasonable supportive advice, but it removes a trigger rather than treating the underlying anxiety and low self esteem.
key_concept:
Adolescent anxiety or low mood: therapy first, drugs second.
  • Mild to moderate: CBT (or other talking therapy).
  • Moderate to severe or failed therapy: add an SSRI (fluoxetine in adolescent depression).
  • Screen use advice is supportive, not the main treatment.
exam_pearl: "Comparing herself with others" is a cognitive distortion, which is what CBT is built to fix.

stem: Elderly patient in 70s Hx of HTN, brought by his son. He stated to forget recent events but remembers old events. He forgets names. He misplaced his items and can't find them, social activities withdrawal due to lack of interest. Mini Mental exam was done and the result was low (i can't remember exactly the number) On MRI: There was cortical atrophy What medication to start?
highlight_terms_source: forget recent events but remembers old events
why_right: An elderly man with recent memory loss but preserved remote memory, forgetting names, misplacing items, withdrawal, a low MMSE and cortical atrophy on MRI has Alzheimer disease. The lead-in asks which medication to start, and first-line drug therapy for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease is a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine), which modestly improves or stabilises cognition and function.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antipsychotics do not treat the cognitive deficit and raise mortality in elderly patients with dementia; they are reserved for severe psychosis or agitation that endangers the patient or others.
B. His withdrawal reflects apathy from dementia, not a depressive episode; an antidepressant is right when there are core depressive features (low mood, guilt) or pseudodementia, not progressive amnestic decline with atrophy.
key_concept:
Alzheimer disease: recent memory lost first, remote memory kept, progressive decline; treat with a cholinesterase inhibitor.
  • Mild to moderate: donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine
  • Moderate to severe: add or use memantine (NMDA antagonist)
  • Imaging first to exclude structural causes; Alzheimer shows cortical and hippocampal atrophy
  • Benign forgetfulness: does not impair daily function
  • Antipsychotics only for dangerous psychosis or agitation
exam_pearl: Social withdrawal in dementia is usually apathy; do not let it pull you toward an antidepressant when the picture is amnestic decline with atrophy.

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains of marked fear whenever dealing with unfamiliar people, as she is afraid of embarrassment. She was referred to a local psychologist for assessment and management. Which of the following will benefit from cognitive behavioral therapy?
highlight_terms_source: marked fear whenever dealing with unfamiliar people
why_right: Marked fear when dealing with unfamiliar people because she is afraid of embarrassment is social phobia (social anxiety disorder). Anxiety disorders are the classic condition where CBT is the first line treatment, using cognitive restructuring and graded exposure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Schizophrenia: treated mainly with antipsychotics; CBT is only an adjunct, and the stem shows no psychotic features.
C. Postpartum psychosis: a psychiatric emergency needing admission and antipsychotics (or ECT), not CBT; she is not postpartum.
D. Depression with hallucination: psychotic depression needs an antidepressant plus antipsychotic or ECT; CBT alone is not appropriate.
key_concept:
CBT is first line where there is no psychosis.
  • Social phobia: fear of scrutiny or embarrassment; CBT, SSRI if needed.
  • Panic disorder, GAD, OCD, phobias: CBT.
  • Psychotic disorders: antipsychotics first; CBT only adjunct.
exam_pearl: Any option containing psychosis or hallucinations is a drug (or ECT) answer, not a CBT answer.

stem: There was a patient with a clinical scenario of Alzheimer's disease prescribed donepezil, but no improvement was noticed for 6 months. MRI showing cortical atrophy. How should his medications be adjusted?
highlight_terms_source: no improvement was noticed for 6 months
why_right: This recall's key is switching donepezil to memantine: the patient with Alzheimer disease has had no improvement after 6 months of donepezil, and MRI shows cortical atrophy (established, progressing disease). The source's reasoning is that the cholinesterase inhibitor has failed, so treatment moves to the other drug class, the NMDA antagonist memantine, which is used in moderate to severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Add sertraline: treats coexisting depression or anxiety in dementia; the stem gives no mood symptoms and it does not treat cognition.
B. Add memantine: combination therapy is used when disease progresses to moderate or severe stage while the cholinesterase inhibitor is still tolerated; this recall keys a switch instead.
D. Switch donepezil to rivastigmine: changing to another cholinesterase inhibitor is mainly for intolerance of donepezil; this key treats the problem as class failure and moves to memantine.
key_concept:
Alzheimer drug ladder.
  • Mild to moderate: cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine).
  • Moderate to severe or AChEI not tolerated: memantine.
  • Already on AChEI and progressing to moderate or severe: memantine can be added.
  • Depression in dementia: SSRI such as sertraline.
exam_pearl: Read the options: switch vs add memantine is the fork, and this recall's key is the switch.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Alzheimer prescribed donepezil for 6 months but no improvement; asking how to adjust his meds (No mention of MMSE drop). Same options; highlighted: C. Change Donepezil To Memantine.

stem: Physician had chronic back pain, prescribed himself oxycodone, present to work, agitated and with pinpoint eyes?
OptA: Something related to stress and burn out
why_right: A physician with chronic back pain who is prescribing himself oxycodone and comes to work agitated with pinpoint pupils shows the opioid picture: miosis is the key sign of opioid effect, and self prescription of a controlled drug is a red flag for misuse. This is drug abuse (opioid overuse), not simple burnout.
why_wrong_block:
A. Something related to stress and burn out: burnout causes exhaustion, cynicism and reduced performance, but does not cause pinpoint pupils; it is the distractor that ignores the physical sign.
C. Option not recalled in the source.
D. Option not recalled in the source.
key_concept:
Pupils separate the toxidromes.
  • Pinpoint (< 2 mm): opioids, also organophosphates (with secretions, bradycardia).
  • Dilated: stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine), anticholinergics, opioid withdrawal.
  • Opioid toxicity: miosis, sedation, respiratory depression.
  • Impaired colleague: ensure patient safety and report through proper channels.
exam_pearl: Self prescribed opioid + pinpoint pupils = opioid misuse; withdrawal would give dilated pupils instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Figure: normal constricted pupil 2-4 mm vs pinpoint pupil <2 mm (miosis).

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a 6-month history of irritability, poor concentration, tension, and anxiety. She is highly active on social media, posting daily. What is the most appropriate initial management?
OptC: Decrease time on the phone to 6 hours
OptD: Encourage her to avoid using social media
why_right: A 17 year old with a 6 month history of irritability, poor concentration, tension and anxiety fits generalized anxiety, linked here to heavy social media use. The lead in is initial management, and in adolescents with anxiety (and no prior treatment) psychological therapy, CBT, is first line before medication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs): added when symptoms are severe or CBT fails or is unavailable; not the initial step here.
C. Decrease time on the phone to 6 hours: an arbitrary limit that does not treat the anxiety; screen advice is only supportive.
D. Encourage her to avoid using social media: removing a trigger without treating the anxiety, and often rejected by adolescents; not the main management.
key_concept:
Adolescent GAD: CBT first.
  • Generalized anxiety: worry, tension, irritability, poor concentration, sleep problems for ≥ 6 months.
  • Initial: CBT.
  • Severe, or no response to CBT: SSRI.
  • Social media limits: supportive advice only.
exam_pearl: "Initial management" in an untreated adolescent with anxiety is CBT; SSRI is the step after.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall: 17-year-old, decreased concentration 6 months, ~9 hours daily on social media, compares herself with others, anxiety and depression, no prior treatment. Options: start antidepressant, force her to leave social media, limit social media time, cognitive behavioral therapy (highlighted).

stem: 25 y/o has difficulty with sleep, sleepy on afternoons. Works on his computer programming at night, has irregular sleep schedule. What to do?
OptB: Regular sleep schedule and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: difficulty with sleep, sleepy on afternoons
why_right: A young programmer who works at night with an irregular sleep schedule and afternoon sleepiness has a behavioural and circadian problem driven by poor sleep hygiene and evening screen light. The first step is to correct the cause: fix a regular sleep and wake time and limit screen exposure before bed.
why_wrong_block: A. CBT for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on most nights for about 3 months despite adequate opportunity); here the problem is a self-imposed irregular schedule, so simple sleep hygiene comes first.
key_concept:
Sleep complaint from an irregular, night-time, screen-heavy routine = fix sleep hygiene first.
  • Fixed wake time and bedtime, including weekends
  • Limit screens and bright light before bed
  • Avoid caffeine later in the day and long daytime naps
  • Chronic insomnia disorder (about 3 months) = CBT-I first line
  • Hypnotics are short term only, never first line
exam_pearl: Clear behavioural trigger (night work, irregular hours, screens) points to sleep hygiene; a documented chronic insomnia disorder points to CBT-I.

stem: A patient with a history of Alzheimer's disease has been on donepezil for 6 months, and no improvement was noticed. His MMSE was 19 (six months ago) and is now 12. MRI shows hippocampus atrophy. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: MMSE was 19 (six months ago) and is now 12
why_right: This patient has Alzheimer disease that has progressed on donepezil (MMSE 19 to 12, now moderate to severe, hippocampal atrophy). The next step is to add memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, to the cholinesterase inhibitor; combination therapy is recommended for moderate to severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sertraline treats comorbid depression, which is not described; it does not slow cognitive decline.
C. Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor with the same mechanism as donepezil; two drugs of the same class are never combined. Switching to it is an option when donepezil is not tolerated, not when the disease has progressed.
D. Stopping donepezil removes a drug that still offers benefit; memantine is added, not substituted, in moderate to severe disease. Switching to memantine alone fits intolerance or contraindication to cholinesterase inhibitors.
key_concept:
Alzheimer drug ladder: cholinesterase inhibitor first, then add memantine as disease becomes moderate to severe.
  • Mild to moderate: donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine
  • Moderate to severe: add memantine to the cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Never combine two cholinesterase inhibitors
  • Switch within class only for intolerance
exam_pearl: Progression on donepezil means add memantine; side effects on donepezil mean switch.

stem: 29 year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with slurred speech. She has a known history of depression and alcohol use disorder, and she reports occasional cravings for mariuana. On exam, she is drowsy, slurring her words, and smells of alcohol. Vitals are stable. Which of the following is the best next step?
why_right: A drowsy patient with slurred speech who smells of alcohol must not be assumed to be simply intoxicated. Alcohol use disorder raises the risk of falls and subdural haematoma, and intoxication can mask a stroke or intracranial bleed, so with an altered level of consciousness and a neurological sign the best next step among these options is a head CT to exclude a structural cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. A urine drug screen looks for co-ingestants (relevant with depression and other substance use) but cannot exclude an intracranial lesion; this key prioritises ruling out a structural cause first.
B. Liver function tests assess chronic alcohol damage but do not explain acute drowsiness and slurred speech; they belong in the later work-up.
C. TSH is irrelevant to an acute change in consciousness; it is checked for chronic fatigue, cognitive slowing or a depressive picture.
key_concept:
Altered consciousness with alcohol on the breath: exclude dangerous causes before blaming alcohol.
  • Check glucose at the bedside
  • Head CT for drowsiness with neurological signs, trauma risk or no improvement as alcohol clears
  • Chronic alcohol use: risk of subdural haematoma and Wernicke encephalopathy (give thiamine)
  • Drug screen and LFTs are secondary
exam_pearl: The smell of alcohol is not a diagnosis; a drinker with slurred speech and drowsiness needs a structural cause excluded.

stem: 63-year-old man presents with multiple psychiatric symptoms, including prominent visual hallucinations. He started on donepezil, which improved his cognition but visual hallucinations persist. what to add?
why_right: Cognition improved on donepezil but prominent visual hallucinations persist. When hallucinations remain distressing despite a cholinesterase inhibitor, a low-dose atypical antipsychotic is added, and quetiapine is preferred because its weak dopamine D2 blockade makes it least likely to worsen parkinsonism or cause severe sensitivity reactions, particularly if this is dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations are a core feature.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sertraline treats depression or anxiety, not psychotic symptoms; it is right if the dominant problem is low mood.
C. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic with strong anticholinergic effects that worsen confusion and can provoke hallucinations in dementia, and it opposes donepezil; it is used for neuropathic pain or depression in younger patients.
D. Donepezil has improved his cognition and cholinesterase inhibitors can reduce hallucinations in Lewy body disease, so stopping it removes benefit; it is stopped for intolerance.
key_concept:
Persistent hallucinations in dementia despite a cholinesterase inhibitor: add a low-dose atypical antipsychotic, quetiapine preferred.
  • DLB: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder
  • DLB patients are very sensitive to antipsychotics; avoid typicals such as haloperidol
  • Quetiapine or clozapine have the least D2 blockade
  • Avoid anticholinergic drugs (tricyclics) in dementia
exam_pearl: In dementia with hallucinations, haloperidol is the trap; quetiapine is the safer choice.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original typed recall: Alzheimer's scenario on donepezil, full improvement after 6 months but still visual hallucinations, how to adjust meds; options ADD quetiapine / ADD amitryptaline / Switch donepezil to rivastigmine; ADD quetiapine highlighted. Q: version states Answer: B.

stem: 45-year-old man with recurrent episodes of schizophrenia is on maintenance therapy to maintain suppression of symptoms, prevent relapse, improve quality of life, and support engagement in psychosocial therapy. Which of the following is the best outcome following the maintenance therapy?
OptC: 70% will have a satisfactory quality of life
why_right: Long-term outcome in schizophrenia follows the rule of thirds: about one third achieve lasting symptom reduction and good function, one third have a relapsing course with partial recovery, and one third remain chronically impaired. So even with good maintenance therapy, the best realistic outcome stated here is that about 33% obtain long-lasting symptom reduction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Complete resolution is not the expected outcome of maintenance therapy; its goals are symptom suppression and relapse prevention, and most patients keep some residual symptoms.
B. 5% understates outcomes; roughly a third do well, so remission is far more common than this.
C. 70% with satisfactory quality of life overstates outcomes; only about a third do well in the long term, and the rest have relapses or chronic impairment.
key_concept:
Schizophrenia prognosis, rule of thirds.
  • About one third: lasting improvement
  • About one third: relapsing course, partial recovery
  • About one third: chronic, severe impairment
  • Good prognosis: acute onset, late onset, clear trigger, positive symptoms, mood symptoms, good premorbid function, female sex, social support
  • Stopping maintenance antipsychotics sharply raises relapse risk
exam_pearl: Schizophrenia outcome questions: think in thirds, not cure.

stem: A 55-year-old man known to have psychiatric disease and hypertension was admitted to the hospital due to poor nutrition at home, as he was refusing food. During hospitalization, he became agitated, so they increased the dose of Haloperidol. Suddenly, he became confused and began sweating. He was shifted to the ICU, started on IV fluids, and intubated (see lab result). Which of the following should be added to the management plan?
why_right: Haloperidol is a potent dopamine antagonist, and the dose was increased just before he suddenly became confused and began sweating, needing ICU care and intubation. This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome: hyperthermia, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability, usually with a markedly raised CK on labs. Beyond stopping the antipsychotic, cooling and IV fluids, the specific drug therapy is a dopamine agonist, bromocriptine (dantrolene is the other option).
why_wrong_block:
A. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, coma); there is no opioid exposure and sweating is not an opioid feature.
B. Glucagon is the antidote for beta blocker (or calcium channel blocker) overdose and treats hypoglycemia; it has no role in NMS.
C. Meropenem is for severe bacterial sepsis; the confusion and sweating here follow the haloperidol dose increase and are drug induced, not infection, although sepsis should be excluded.
key_concept:
NMS = dopamine blockade → treat with dopamine agonist.
  • Triggers: antipsychotics (haloperidol), metoclopramide, abrupt stop of levodopa
  • Features: lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, confusion, autonomic instability
  • Labs: high CK, leukocytosis, possible myoglobinuria / AKI
  • Treat: stop drug, cooling, IV fluids, bromocriptine or dantrolene
  • Serotonin syndrome instead: clonus, hyperreflexia, rapid onset → cyproheptadine
exam_pearl: Antipsychotic + rigidity + fever + confusion = NMS (bromocriptine); SSRI + clonus = serotonin syndrome (cyproheptadine).

stem: Young female with history of lack of sleep, decreased appetite, decreased concentration, loss of interest in activities and isolation. Which of the following is the most concerning?
OptA: Loss of interest in previously interesting activity
why_right: This young woman has depressive symptoms, and most concerning means the feature that most raises suicide risk. Isolation and social withdrawal (lack of social support) is an established suicide risk factor in depression, while the other options are core depressive symptoms that confirm the diagnosis but carry less risk on their own.
why_wrong_block:
A. Loss of interest (anhedonia) is a core symptom that helps diagnose depression, but it is not singled out as a suicide risk marker the way isolation is.
C. Changes in appetite and sleep are neurovegetative features of depression; they support the diagnosis but are not the most concerning risk feature.
D. Decreased concentration is a common depressive symptom affecting function but does not by itself signal high suicide risk.
key_concept:
Most concerning in depression = the feature that raises suicide risk; social isolation tops these options.
  • SAD PERSONS: Sex male, Age (young or elderly), Depression, Previous attempt, Ethanol or drugs, Rational thinking lost, Social support lacking, Organised plan, No spouse, Sickness
  • Women attempt more, men complete more
  • Always ask directly about suicidal thoughts
exam_pearl: If an option names a plan, previous attempt or suicidal thoughts, that outranks isolation.

stem: A 27 year old lady complaining of dysmenorrhea during menstruation. Now she start complaining of irritability, insomnia and suicidal thoughts thet start before menstruation by 5 days. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Mood symptoms (irritability, insomnia) that start about 5 days before menstruation are tied to the luteal phase. When the affective symptoms are severe, here suicidal thoughts, the diagnosis is premenstrual dysphoric disorder, the severe mood-dominant form of PMS. The dysmenorrhea is incidental.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bipolar disorder has manic or hypomanic episodes lasting days to weeks not linked to the cycle; here symptoms recur only before menses.
B. Generalised anxiety disorder is excessive worry on most days for at least 6 months, not cyclic premenstrual symptoms.
C. Perimenopausal depression occurs near menopause (usually mid-40s or later) with irregular cycles and vasomotor symptoms; she is 27.
key_concept:
Luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menses: PMS if mild to moderate, PMDD if mood symptoms are severe.
  • Onset in the week before menses, resolves within the first few days of menses
  • PMDD: marked irritability, depression, anxiety or lability with functional impairment
  • Clinical diagnosis, confirmed by a prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles
  • Treatment: lifestyle, then SSRI (best evidence), then combined OCP
exam_pearl: Timing makes the diagnosis: symptoms confined to the premenstrual week point to PMS or PMDD whatever the mood symptom.

stem: He has difficulty maintaining sleep for the last 3 months. His irregular sleep pattern was documented in his diary. I forgot the exact stem but it was like what is the most appropriate advise for his sleep health?
OptC: Regular sleep schedule and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: difficulty maintaining sleep for the last 3 months
why_right: Difficulty maintaining sleep for 3 months, documented in a sleep diary, meets chronic insomnia disorder. First-line treatment for chronic insomnia is CBT for insomnia (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive therapy), which works better long term than medication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Afternoon caffeine worsens sleep onset and maintenance; caffeine should be avoided later in the day.
C. A regular schedule and limiting screens are sleep hygiene, which is only one part of CBT-I and not enough alone for chronic insomnia; it is the answer when a behavioural cause is the whole problem without established chronic insomnia.
D. Sedative hypnotics are short-term adjuncts only, with tolerance, dependence and falls risk; they are not first line.
key_concept:
Chronic insomnia disorder (about 3 months, diary confirmed) = CBT-I first line.
  • CBT-I: stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring
  • Sleep hygiene alone: fine for simple behavioural sleep problems
  • Hypnotics: short term, lowest dose
  • Screen for depression, OSA, drugs and caffeine
exam_pearl: Duration flips the answer: about 3 months of insomnia means CBT-I, not just sleep hygiene advice.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with a 2-year history of depression presents to the clinic for followup. Her husband raised a concern about suicide as she is looking more depressed and isolated recently. She denied any history of alcohol or psychoactive substance use. During her clinical exam, there was no eye contact and her systemic exams were unremarkable. Which of the following risk factors carries the highest risk for suicide?
why_right: In a woman with depression who is now more depressed and isolated, social isolation (lack of social support, living alone, withdrawal) is the strongest risk factor among the options. The others either do not apply to her (age 38, female) or are protective (no serious illness).
why_wrong_block:
A. Suicide risk is highest in older patients (and adolescents); 38 is not a high-risk age.
B. Women attempt suicide more often, but men complete suicide more often, so female sex is not the highest-risk factor.
D. Chronic or terminal illness raises suicide risk; its absence is not a risk factor.
key_concept:
Suicide risk factors (SAD PERSONS).
  • Sex male, Age older (or adolescent)
  • Depression, Previous attempt
  • Ethanol/substance use, Rational thinking lost (psychosis)
  • Social support lacking (isolation), Organized plan
  • No spouse, Sickness (chronic illness)
  • Strongest single predictor overall: previous attempt
exam_pearl: Women attempt more, men complete more; among her own features, isolation is the danger sign.

stem: Man 6 months after bariatric surgery successfully losing weight and adherent to his diet and exercise but he is worried about long term success, he is at which of the following stages?
highlight_terms_source: adherent to his diet and exercise
why_right: The transtheoretical (stages of change) model labels a person who has sustained the new behaviour for about 6 months or longer as being in maintenance. He is "6 months after" surgery, is "successfully losing weight" and "adherent" to diet and exercise, and his concern is now "long term success", which is exactly the task of maintenance: preventing relapse. So the key is maintenance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Action: the first months (under about 6) of actively doing the new behaviour. He has passed that window and is now focused on keeping the change, not starting it.
C. Contemplation: aware of the problem and thinking about changing within the next months but not yet acting. He is already acting consistently.
D. Pre-contemplation: no intention to change and often denies the problem. He has had surgery and changed his lifestyle, so this clearly does not fit.
key_concept:
Stages of change: identify where the patient is by intention and by how long the change has lasted.
  • Pre-contemplation: no intention to change
  • Contemplation: considering change, ambivalent
  • Preparation: planning, small steps, change imminent
  • Action: actively changing, under about 6 months
  • Maintenance: change sustained about 6 months or more, focus on relapse prevention
  • Relapse: return to old behaviour, can re-enter the cycle
exam_pearl: The 6 month mark separates action from maintenance; worry about keeping the change long term points to maintenance.

stem: Patient presents with depression, loss of appetite, start isolation from people, and want to use of marijuana to relieve stress . They also show anxiety and depression drug no compliance. (On examination she was Unkempt with slurred speech.) What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_right: She uses marijuana "to relieve stress", is unkempt with "slurred speech" and is not taking her psychiatric drugs, so substance intoxication or use must be excluded first. A urine drug screen is quick, cheap and directly tests the most likely contributor to her depressive picture and neurological sign. Substance use changes the diagnosis (substance induced mood disorder) and the management, so it is the most appropriate initial test.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: useful when anemia or infection could explain fatigue, but nothing here points to it, and it does not explain slurred speech with cannabis use.
C. Pulmonary function test: would be relevant for chronic respiratory symptoms in a smoker, not for evaluating a mood and behaviour change.
D. Thyroid function test: part of the routine organic workup of new depression, but here the clear clue is substance use with slurred speech, so the drug screen comes first.
key_concept:
Psychiatric presentation with a substance clue: screen for the substance before labelling a primary disorder.
  • Slurred speech, unkempt, reported drug use: urine drug screen
  • New depression without clues: TFT, CBC, basic labs to exclude organic causes
  • Positive screen: consider substance induced mood disorder
exam_pearl: When the stem names a substance and shows an intoxication sign (slurred speech), the urine drug screen beats the routine organic labs.

stem: Female patient came 2 weeks after delivery with mood swings and feeling overwhelmed, she has no thought to harm herself or her baby. She is breastfeeding. She has good social support. What to do?
OptD: encourage her (or support her) and follow up her
highlight_terms_source: no thought to harm herself or her baby
why_right: Mood swings and feeling overwhelmed in the first 2 weeks after delivery, with "no thought to harm herself or her baby" and "good social support", fit postpartum (baby) blues. Blues is self limiting and usually settles within about 2 weeks, so treatment is support and advice, with follow up to make sure symptoms resolve and do not evolve into postpartum depression. This is why "support her and follow up" is better than reassurance alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stop breastfeeding: never needed for blues, and even in postpartum depression many antidepressants are compatible with breastfeeding.
B. Reassure: correct in spirit, but reassurance alone omits follow up. At 2 weeks, persisting symptoms would point to postpartum depression, so she must be reviewed.
C. Antidepressants: right for postpartum depression (symptoms beyond 2 weeks, anhedonia, guilt, functional impairment), not for short lived blues.
key_concept:
Postpartum mood disorders are separated mainly by timing, duration and severity.
  • Baby blues: starts in the first days, lasts up to about 2 weeks, mild, function preserved: support, education, follow up
  • Postpartum depression: persists beyond 2 weeks, anhedonia, guilt, impaired function: psychotherapy with or without SSRI
  • Postpartum psychosis: hallucinations, delusions, confusion: emergency admission
exam_pearl: Duration is the discriminator: symptoms still present past 2 weeks are no longer blues, so blues always needs follow up.

  • Management: mood stabilizer or antipsychotic, stop antidepressant

stem: Elderly pt~ 70y/o after elective orthopedic surgery was in icu when he wakes up was alert but confused asking "where I'm?" And trying to remove the canula, what to do:
OptC: keep assuring him and adequate lighting
why_right: An elderly patient waking in ICU after surgery who is alert but "confused", disoriented ("where am I?") and pulling at the cannula has postoperative delirium. First line management is non pharmacological: reorientation and reassurance, adequate lighting, glasses and hearing aids, presence of family, normal sleep wake cycle, plus searching for and correcting the cause. Drugs are kept for distress or danger that does not settle with these measures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haloperidol: low dose short term use is right when agitation is severe and dangerous to the patient or staff despite non drug measures; not as the first step.
B. Quetiapine: an antipsychotic alternative when one is needed, preferred in Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia where haloperidol worsens symptoms; still second line after non drug care.
key_concept:
Delirium: treat the cause and start with non drug measures.
  • Reorient, reassure, family presence, clock and calendar
  • Good lighting by day, dark and quiet at night, glasses and hearing aids
  • Look for cause: infection, drugs, pain, retention, hypoxia, electrolytes
  • Severe dangerous agitation: low dose haloperidol, short term
  • Avoid benzodiazepines unless alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
exam_pearl: Pulling at lines alone does not justify sedation; only harm that persists after non drug measures does.

stem: Elderly with UTI and suspected urosepsis admitted 2 days later he developed acute confusion with fluctuations in awareness, he was AGITATED what to do??

Delirium = acute onset, fluctuating attention and awareness, usually from a medical cause.
  • Treat the cause (here the UTI and sepsis)
  • Non drug measures first: sleep cycle, reorientation, lighting, aids, family
  • Antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation
  • Avoid restraint and benzodiazepines
exam_pearl: "Agitated" tempts you to sedate, but exams reward non drug measures plus treating the cause unless there is danger.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with insomnia, fatigue, and sadness. She delivered her first child 5 days ago. Examination reveals a tearful and depressed appearance. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: delivered her first child 5 days ago
why_right: This recall's key reads the "tearful and depressed appearance" with insomnia, fatigue and sadness after her first delivery as postpartum depression, so it is treated rather than watched. An SSRI (sertraline is preferred, as it is compatible with breastfeeding) is the first line drug treatment, combined with psychological support.
why_wrong_block:
B. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, cause sedation and dependence, and pass into breast milk; they are not a treatment for postpartum mood disorders.
C. Follow-up in 1 week is the plan for postpartum blues (mild, transient low mood starting around days 3 to 5 and resolving within 2 weeks); the key treats this presentation as depression needing treatment, so watchful waiting alone is not chosen.
D. Multivitamins have no role in treating postpartum mood symptoms.
key_concept:
Postpartum mood spectrum: decide by timing, duration and severity.
  • Blues: days 3 to 5, resolves within 2 weeks = reassure, follow up
  • Depression: symptoms beyond 2 weeks or severe = SSRI (sertraline) plus psychotherapy
  • Psychosis: first 2 weeks, hallucinations, delusions, confusion = admit, antipsychotic
  • Any thoughts of harm to self or baby = urgent psychiatry
exam_pearl: Mild, transient low mood in the first 2 weeks = blues (reassure, follow up); a depressive picture needing treatment = SSRI, sertraline if breastfeeding.
