stem: A 70-year-old man complains that he cannot remember things, sometimes forgetting names of friends, famous community figures, and telephone numbers. His wife fears he has Alzheimer's disease. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from tender knee joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: forgetting names of friends, famous community figures, and telephone numbers
why_right: He sometimes forgets names and telephone numbers, with no reported impairment of daily function, no other cognitive or behavioral symptoms and an unremarkable examination (tender knees are incidental). Occasional retrieval lapses with preserved function are normal age-associated (benign) forgetfulness, not dementia. The worry comes from the wife, not from functional decline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Alzheimer disease is right when progressive memory loss for recent events interferes with daily activities (getting lost, repeating questions, failing to manage finances); none of that is described.
B. Lewy body dementia is right with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or REM sleep behavior disorder; none is present here.
D. Hypertensive encephalopathy is an acute emergency with severe hypertension, headache, confusion, seizures or visual changes; it is not a chronic mild memory complaint with a normal exam.
key_concept:
Dementia needs cognitive decline that impairs daily function.
  • Benign forgetfulness: occasional lapses, later recalled, function intact
  • Alzheimer: insidious recent memory loss, functional decline
  • Lewy body: fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
  • Vascular: stepwise or executive dysfunction, vascular risk factors
  • NPH: gait disturbance, incontinence, confusion
exam_pearl: The patient complaining about his own memory (rather than family noticing decline) with intact function favors benign forgetfulness.

stem: Lady in the 70s has type 2 DM on metformin 1 g BID had problems in naming and calling things lately.For example, she says animal instead of "cat" when she sees a cat. She has no memory impairment or personality changes. Her family is worried about her. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: problems in naming and calling things
no memory impairment or personality changes
why_right: The decisive clue is isolated naming difficulty with loss of word meaning (she says "animal" instead of "cat") while memory and personality are preserved. This is the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (semantic dementia), which falls under the frontotemporal dementia spectrum. FTD presents with either a behavioral picture or a language picture, and the language variants spare episodic memory early.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vascular dementia: stepwise decline with focal deficits, stroke history and early executive dysfunction. Diabetes is a risk factor, but nothing focal or stepwise is described.
B. Alzheimer's dementia: starts with recent (episodic) memory loss; language problems come later. Here memory is explicitly normal.
D. B12 deficiency with cognitive features: metformin can lower B12, but deficiency gives global cognitive slowing or memory problems with neuropathy, ataxia or anemia, not an isolated loss of word meaning.
key_concept:
Dementia type is decided by the FIRST domain affected.
  • Recent memory first: Alzheimer
  • Behavior/disinhibition or language first, memory spared: frontotemporal
  • Stepwise, focal signs, executive dysfunction: vascular
  • Fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism: Lewy body
  • Gait + incontinence + cognition: NPH
exam_pearl: Anomia with lost word meaning and normal memory points to FTD (semantic variant); do not let the metformin detail pull you to B12.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with 2-year history of slow and progressive deterioration in his memory. The patient is able to perform some activities of daily living, including dressing and bathing. His personality has changed from that of a kind and caring person into someone who has periods of agitation and aggression. Neurologic and musculoskeletal examination cannot be carried out. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 2-year history of slow and progressive deterioration in his memory
why_right: A 78-year-old with a 2-year slow, progressive decline that starts with memory fits Alzheimer's disease, the most common dementia. Personality change with agitation and aggression appears as the disease advances, and the gradual (not stepwise) course with no vascular history supports it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mixed dementia: needs evidence of both Alzheimer and cerebrovascular disease (strokes, stepwise decline, imaging changes); nothing vascular is given.
C. Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors; here the course is smooth and slow.
D. Major depressive disorder: can mimic dementia (pseudodementia) but has prominent low mood, anhedonia and subacute onset; it does not cause a steady 2-year memory decline with aggression.
key_concept:
Alzheimer = insidious, gradually progressive, memory first.
  • Early: recent memory loss
  • Later: language, visuospatial, personality change, agitation
  • Stepwise + focal signs: think vascular
  • Mood symptoms leading the picture: think depression
exam_pearl: Smooth progressive decline beginning with memory is Alzheimer; a stepwise course would flip it to vascular.

stem: 7-year-old child who is the only child of his parents He refuses the school or his parents refuse "something like that" What to do?
OptA: Delay his school by one year.
why_right: A 7-year-old only child refusing school (with possibly anxious parents) suggests school refusal driven by separation anxiety. Management is behavioral: early, gradual (gentle) separation and return to school with parental support and reassurance, ideally with cognitive behavioral techniques. Avoidance reinforces the anxiety.
why_wrong_block:
A. Delay his school by one year: keeping the child away rewards avoidance and makes the anxiety worse; the goal is early return to school.
B. Study at home: again an avoidance strategy that removes the child from peers and school and entrenches the problem.
C. Give anxiety medication: drugs (SSRIs) are reserved for severe or refractory anxiety after behavioral therapy fails, not first line in a young child.
key_concept:
School refusal / separation anxiety = behavioral management, not avoidance.
  • Reassure and educate parents
  • Gradual separation and early return to school
  • CBT with exposure
  • SSRI only if severe or refractory
exam_pearl: Any option that keeps the child home (delay, home study) is wrong; graded return is the answer.

stem: A 65-year-old man with congestive heart failure and osteoarthritis moved into a nursing home 3 months ago. During the past 4 weeks, the patient has lost 3.6 kg, lost interest in all social activities, and has been crying almost every day. The mood is worse in the morning. At times, especially when the mood is impaired, the patient's short-term memory appears to be lost. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: lost interest in all social activities
mood is worse in the morning
when the mood is impaired, the patient's short-term memory appears to be lost
why_right: After a major life change (moving to a nursing home) he has 4 weeks of weight loss, loss of interest, daily crying and mood worse in the morning. These are features of a major depressive episode, and the memory loss that appears when the mood is low is depressive pseudodementia, which improves when the depression is treated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise cognitive decline with focal deficits; memory loss would not wax and wane with mood.
B. Alzheimer's disease: insidious, progressive memory loss over years, with mood change appearing later; not a 4-week mood syndrome with mood-linked forgetfulness.
C. Hypothyroidism: can cause low mood and slowing, but typically with weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation; here he is losing weight.
key_concept:
Pseudodementia (depression) vs dementia:
  • Depression: subacute onset, mood symptoms first, memory fluctuates with mood, "I don't know" answers
  • Dementia: insidious onset, memory first, patient minimizes deficits
  • Diurnal variation (worse in morning) favors depression
exam_pearl: Memory loss that worsens with low mood in an elderly person after a life change is depression, not dementia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version options: A. Alzheimer's disease, B. Depression, C. Multiple infarction dementia (memory loss fluctuates with mood). Answer: D refers to the Q: version (Depression).

stem: 25 years old man presented to the clinic and he seems to be looking frequently at the corner of the room when asked he said “my mother is standing there, but others can’t see her only me”. When relatives from his family were asked they said that his mother died when he was 5 years old. What does he have or what is the cause of this?
highlight_terms_source: my mother is standing there, but others can’t see her only me
why_right: He sees his mother standing in the corner when no one else can, and she died years ago. A perception without an external stimulus is a hallucination, and since the modality is sight (he keeps looking at the corner), it is a visual hallucination.
why_wrong_block:
B. Auditory hallucinations: hearing voices without a stimulus; he describes seeing her, not hearing her.
C. Episode of disorganized thoughts: a disorder of thought form (derailment, loose associations, incoherent speech); his answer is clear and goal directed.
D. Delusion: a fixed false belief (a thought problem), not a sensory perception; it would be a delusion if he believed she was alive without perceiving her.
key_concept:
Perception vs belief vs thought form:
  • Hallucination: perception without stimulus (visual, auditory, tactile...)
  • Illusion: misinterpretation of a real stimulus
  • Delusion: fixed false belief
  • Disorganized thinking: abnormal thought form
exam_pearl: "I see her but others can't" is a perception, so hallucination; name the modality from the sense used.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version (screenshot on next page): 27-year-old kept looking to the right, 'My mother is there, but no one can see her except me', she comes and goes, family says she died when he was a child; options A. Delusion, **B. Visual hallucination, C. Auditory hallucination, D. Episode of disorganized thinking. Same answer (visual hallucination).

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with history of hearing voices coming from the toaster and refrigerator, warning that all the food is poisoned. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: He hears voices coming from the toaster and refrigerator. Hearing voices with no real speaker is a perception without a stimulus in the auditory modality, so the core phenomenon is an auditory hallucination, the most common type in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Delusional thinking: a fixed false belief. Believing the food is poisoned could be a secondary delusion, but the question describes the voices themselves, which are a perceptual disturbance.
B. Visual hallucination: would require seeing things that are not there; he hears, not sees.
C. Disorganized thinking: loose associations or incoherent speech; nothing about his thought form is described.
key_concept:
Classify the psychotic symptom by what is abnormal:
  • A sense (heard, seen, felt): hallucination of that modality
  • A belief (poisoned, followed): delusion
  • The flow of thought: disorganization
  • Auditory is the commonest hallucination in schizophrenia; visual suggests organic causes
exam_pearl: Voices from objects = auditory hallucination; the poisoning content tempts you to pick delusion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot only; **D marked (the word 'Delusional' in option A has a blue selection highlight, not the answer mark).

stem: Psyco insomnia hx depressive family hx of mania presents with symptoms of insomnia and maybe irritability?

Insomnia in a patient with a mood history: decide which sleep problem it is.

  • Low mood + anhedonia + insomnia ≥2 weeks: depression, treat after bipolar screen
  • Little sleep but full of energy, irritable: hypomania/mania, mood stabilizer
  • Family history of mania: avoid antidepressant monotherapy

stem: An 82-year-old man hospitalized for a severe urinary tract infection develops acute confusion, agitation, and a fluctuating level of consciousness. He is diagnosed with delirium. In addition to treating his underlying infection, what is the most appropriate next step in his supportive management?
OptB: Reorient the patient frequently to time and place
OptC: Apply physical restraints to prevent accidental falls
OptD: Place the patient in a dark, completely isolated room
highlight_terms_source: acute confusion, agitation, and a fluctuating level of consciousness
why_right: Delirium is managed by treating the cause (here the UTI) plus non-pharmacological supportive care, which is first line. Frequent reorientation to time and place (clocks, calendars, familiar faces), a calm lit room by day, normal sleep cycle, glasses and hearing aids reduce confusion and agitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Initiate low-dose haloperidol therapy: reserved for severe agitation that endangers the patient or staff after non-drug measures fail; not routine supportive care.
C. Apply physical restraints to prevent accidental falls: restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium duration; use only as a last resort for immediate danger.
D. Place the patient in a dark, completely isolated room: sensory deprivation and isolation worsen disorientation; the room should be well lit by day with familiar people present.
key_concept:
Delirium management ladder:
  • 1. Find and treat the cause (infection, drugs, metabolic)
  • 2. Non-drug measures: reorientation, family, glasses/hearing aids, sleep hygiene, mobilization
  • 3. Low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation
  • Avoid restraints, benzodiazepines (except alcohol withdrawal) and isolation
exam_pearl: "Supportive management" in delirium means reorientation; haloperidol is the trap unless agitation is dangerous.

stem: A mother was concerned of ADHD in her child (8 years). She described him at home as restless and cannot focus. Upon your assessment he is a calm child with normal behavior. What is the best action:
OptA: Obtain further information from parents and teachers
OptB: Start him on trial of amphetamines
OptC: Reassure the mother that these are normal behaviors at his age
why_right: ADHD diagnosis requires symptoms in at least two settings (home and school) that impair function. The mother reports symptoms at home, but the child is calm in the clinic, and office behavior is not reliable. The next step is to gather information from parents and teachers, usually with standardized rating scales, before diagnosing or treating.
why_wrong_block:
B. Start him on trial of amphetamines: stimulants are started only after the diagnosis is confirmed; a therapeutic trial is not a diagnostic test.
C. Reassure the mother that these are normal behaviors at his age: premature; dismissing her report without school information can miss true ADHD. Reassurance fits only after collateral history is normal.
D. Do neurological exam: part of a general assessment to exclude other causes, but it does not establish or refute ADHD, which is a clinical diagnosis based on history across settings.
key_concept:
ADHD is a clinical diagnosis:
  • Symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for ≥6 months
  • Several symptoms present before age 12
  • Present in ≥2 settings (home, school)
  • Collect rating scales from parents AND teachers
  • Normal clinic behavior does not exclude ADHD
exam_pearl: A calm child in clinic does not rule out ADHD; get the teacher's report.

stem: 7-year-old child is reported to be hyperactive, restless, talks rapidly, and has violent outbursts. What intervention can help mitigate these issues?
OptB: Decreasing time spent on video games and watching television
why_right: A school age child who is "hyperactive, restless, talks rapidly" with "violent outbursts" fits ADHD with disruptive behavior. The lead-in asks what intervention helps mitigate these behaviors, and parent training in behavior management (rewarding positive behavior, planned ignoring, consistent limits and consequences) is the core non-drug intervention that reduces hyperactivity and aggression at home. It is the only option that directly targets the behavior itself.
why_wrong_block:
A. Preschool examinations are screening visits, not a treatment; this child is 7 and already of school age, so they do nothing to change his behavior.
B. Cutting screen time is reasonable general advice but has no proven effect as a treatment for ADHD symptoms or aggression; it would only be a supportive add on.
D. Special education resources are for a child with a learning disability or academic failure; nothing in the stem describes school performance problems, and they do not address outbursts at home.
key_concept:
ADHD behavior: parent training in behavior management is the first non-drug step.
  • Techniques: reward positive behavior, ignore minor disruptive behavior, time out, clear consistent rules
  • Preschool age: parent training is first line before medication
  • School age: stimulant medication plus behavioral therapy and school support
  • Toddler tantrums: reinforce positive behavior, no drugs
exam_pearl: When the stem asks for an intervention for a child's disruptive behavior, pick the option that trains the parents in behavior management, not a screening visit or general lifestyle advice.

stem: 79-year-old male patient, post cholecystectomy, developed confusion and agitation. What to do?
why_right: An elderly patient who becomes acutely "confused and agitated" after surgery has postoperative delirium. First line management is to treat the cause and use non-pharmacological measures, of which reorientation (clock, calendar, familiar faces, glasses and hearing aids, explaining where they are) is the key step. Drugs and restraints are reserved for when these fail and the patient is a danger to self or others.
why_wrong_block:
A. Physical restraint worsens agitation, prolongs delirium and causes injury; it is a last resort only for immediate danger when other measures fail.
B. A quiet room alone is part of the environmental care but isolation without orientation cues can worsen confusion; orientation is the active intervention asked for.
C. Antipsychotics (e.g. low dose haloperidol) are used only when non-drug measures fail and agitation is severe or dangerous; they are not the first step in an elderly patient.
key_concept:
Delirium management ladder: find and treat the cause, then non-drug measures, then drugs only if dangerous.
  • Search for cause: infection, hypoxia, electrolytes, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), urinary retention, pain
  • Non-drug: reorientation, family presence, glasses and hearing aids, sleep and day/night cues, early mobilization
  • Severe agitation with risk of harm: low dose antipsychotic
  • Avoid benzodiazepines (except alcohol withdrawal) and physical restraints
exam_pearl: In delirium questions, "give antipsychotic" and "restrain" are traps when the patient is not yet a danger; orientation and non-drug measures come first.

stem: A female patient presents with decreased need for sleep, increased energy, and rapid speech. What is the most appropriate treatment? No Any Other Feature Mentioned In The Recall , Just Acute Mania (No Obesity , DLP , HTN , Etc Not “Mentioned” )
highlight_terms_source: decreased need for sleep, increased energy, and rapid speech
key_concept:
Acute mania: lithium, valproate or a second generation antipsychotic are all first line options; stop any antidepressant.
  • Severe agitation or psychosis: antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) for fast control
  • Classic euphoric mania and maintenance: lithium
  • Mixed features or rapid cycling: valproate often preferred
  • Pregnancy: avoid valproate
  • Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder is contraindicated
exam_pearl: Decide with the lead-in words: "rapid control" or agitation points to an antipsychotic, "mood stabilizer" or maintenance points to lithium, and an SSRI is never the answer in mania.

stem: Old age with 2 year history of progressive memory loss, had multiple attacks of weakness, decline in abilities and cognitive function, he was diagnosed with HIV 3 years ago, diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clue is "multiple attacks of weakness": repeated focal neurological events (strokes or TIAs) with progressive "decline in abilities and cognitive function" describe the stepwise course of vascular dementia. The HIV history is a distractor; nothing suggests uncontrolled HIV or the subcortical motor slowing of HIV dementia, while the focal attacks point to cerebrovascular disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. Lewy body dementia needs fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations or parkinsonism, none of which are described.
C. Alzheimer disease causes gradual memory loss without focal attacks of weakness; it would be right if the decline were smooth with no neurological events.
D. HIV related dementia is a subcortical picture (slowing, apathy, motor slowing) in poorly controlled HIV with low CD4; the stem's focal attacks of weakness point instead to strokes.
key_concept:
Dementia types by key clue:
  • Vascular: stepwise decline, focal deficits, vascular risk factors (HTN, DM), early executive dysfunction and gait problems
  • Alzheimer: gradual recent memory loss first, no focal signs, most common overall
  • Lewy body: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
  • HIV associated: subcortical slowing, apathy, motor slowing; mainly with uncontrolled HIV and low CD4
  • NPH: gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
exam_pearl: Episodes of focal weakness plus cognitive decline means vascular dementia, even when another tempting cause like HIV is mentioned.

stem: A 70-year-old male presents with a 2-year history of slow and progressive memory loss. He has a history of hypertension, diabetes, and multiple Attacks Of Weakness. It was discovered 3 years ago that he has HIV through routine screening, he use his medication. He also exhibits apraxia, abnormal gait, and otherneurological symptoms. What is the diagnosis? Examiner Said: I believe TIA was not mentioned by word
why_right: A 70-year-old with "hypertension, diabetes" (vascular risk factors), "multiple attacks of weakness" (focal events consistent with strokes or TIAs), plus "apraxia, abnormal gait" and other neurological signs alongside memory loss fits vascular dementia. The HIV is screen detected and treated (the stem says he takes his medication), which makes HIV associated dementia much less likely than cerebrovascular disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lewy body dementia requires fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations or parkinsonism; none are described.
B. Alzheimer disease is gradual memory loss without focal neurological attacks or early gait disturbance; the vascular risk factors and weakness episodes point elsewhere.
C. HIV associated dementia occurs mainly with untreated or poorly controlled HIV and low CD4; this patient is on treatment and the focal attacks of weakness point to strokes.
key_concept:
Dementia types by key clue:
  • Vascular: stepwise decline, focal deficits, vascular risk factors (HTN, DM), early executive dysfunction and gait problems
  • Alzheimer: gradual recent memory loss first, no focal signs, most common overall
  • Lewy body: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
  • HIV associated: subcortical slowing, apathy, motor slowing; mainly with uncontrolled HIV and low CD4
  • NPH: gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
exam_pearl: HTN plus DM plus attacks of focal weakness plus gait problems equals vascular dementia; treated HIV in the stem is a distractor.

stem: 17-year-old girl complained of anorexia nervosa was admitted for initiation of nutrition, the blood samples revealed : hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia. What is the cause of the laboratory investigation?
why_right: A malnourished patient (anorexia nervosa) who develops "hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia" after "initiation of nutrition" has refeeding syndrome. The carbohydrate load triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, so serum levels fall even though total body stores were already depleted.
why_wrong_block:
A. Refeeding syndrome can occur even with a correct protocol in a severely malnourished patient; the lab pattern is a recognized physiological complication, not proof of a wrong regimen (though feeding should be started slowly with electrolyte monitoring).
B. The three low electrolytes fit a known clinical syndrome in this exact setting, so there is no reason to blame the test.
D. A lab kit error would not produce this specific, physiologically consistent triad in a patient just started on feeding.
key_concept:
Refeeding syndrome: low phosphate, low potassium, low magnesium after restarting nutrition in a malnourished patient.
  • At risk: anorexia nervosa, cachexia, prolonged fasting, alcohol use disorder
  • Mechanism: insulin surge shifts electrolytes into cells
  • Hallmark: hypophosphatemia
  • Complications: arrhythmia, heart failure, respiratory failure, weakness, fluid retention
  • Prevention: start feeding low and increase slowly, give thiamine, monitor and replace electrolytes
exam_pearl: Watch for the HYPER versus HYPO trap: refeeding causes hypophosphatemia, never hyperphosphatemia.

stem: Patient old age diabetic (it was a very long scenario) the highlight of the scenario was that he was upon admission conscious, alert and oriented, after a while he became confused (they also imply that he has no cognitive impairment). He was also sick with either pneumonia or UTI (I'm not sure, but it's similar to the question that says a patient is sick with altered level of consciousness and then the answer would be that we initiate antibiotics, it was a similar stem). In the labs sodium was 132. What differentiates the patient's condition from dementia?
highlight_terms_source: after a while he became confused
key_concept:
Delirium versus dementia:
  • Onset: delirium acute (hours to days); dementia insidious (months to years)
  • Course: delirium fluctuates; dementia steadily progressive
  • Consciousness and attention: impaired in delirium; usually preserved in early dementia
  • Cause: delirium has a trigger (infection, electrolytes, drugs, hypoxia); dementia is neurodegenerative or vascular
  • Reversibility: delirium usually reversible once the cause is treated
exam_pearl: Fluctuating consciousness and inattention with an acute trigger point to delirium; insidious onset points to dementia.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: There was patient with clinical scenario of Alzheimer's prescribed donepezil but no improvement was noticed (literally said no improvement, not little, not incomplete) for 6 months. His MMSE was 19 and now is 12. Asking how to adjust his meds:
why_right: This recall's key is to switch donepezil to memantine because the patient had "no improvement" at all on an adequate trial (6 months) while MMSE fell from 19 to 12, now in the moderate range. Treating him as a non-responder, the reasoning is to change drug class to the NMDA antagonist memantine, which is licensed for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, rather than persist with or add to a drug that has failed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sertraline treats depression or anxiety in dementia; there is no mention of mood symptoms and it does not slow cognitive decline.
B. Adding memantine to donepezil is used in moderate to severe disease when the patient is benefiting from or tolerating the cholinesterase inhibitor; the stem stresses complete lack of response, which the key treats as a reason to switch rather than combine.
D. Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor with the same mechanism; switching within the class is mainly for intolerance of donepezil rather than lack of effect, and the decline is now moderate.
key_concept:
Alzheimer drug ladder by severity:
  • Mild to moderate: cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine)
  • Moderate with intolerance or contraindication to cholinesterase inhibitors: memantine
  • Severe: memantine
  • Moderate to severe already on a cholinesterase inhibitor: memantine can be added
  • Rough MMSE bands: mild 21 to 26, moderate 10 to 20, severe below 10
exam_pearl: The stem's emphasis on "no improvement" drives the switch to a different class; with partial benefit the expected move is to add memantine.

stem: A 7 month old pediatric came with convergence and esotropia.and during exam absent corneal light reflex The parents are concerned what should you do?
why_right: A 7-month-old with "convergence and esotropia" and an abnormal corneal light reflex (Hirschberg test) has true strabismus, not pseudostrabismus. Intermittent misalignment is common only in the first few months; a constant deviation at this age needs ophthalmology referral to look for an underlying cause (refractive error, cataract, retinoblastoma) and to prevent amblyopia.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance fits pseudostrabismus, where broad epicanthal folds make the eyes look crossed but the corneal light reflex is symmetric and centered; here the reflex is abnormal, so the strabismus is real.
key_concept:
Infant eye turning: the corneal light reflex decides.
  • Symmetric centered light reflex: pseudostrabismus, reassure
  • Asymmetric or displaced reflex: true strabismus, refer to ophthalmology
  • Esotropia: reflex displaced temporally; exotropia: displaced nasally
  • Most serious complication of untreated strabismus: amblyopia
  • Always check the red reflex too (cataract, retinoblastoma)
exam_pearl: Reassure only when the corneal light reflex is symmetric; any persistent true strabismus beyond early infancy goes to ophthalmology.

stem: 6 month old baby with right esotropia since birth. Absent red light reflex in right eye and negative cover/uncover test. What is the management?
why_right: The decisive clue is an "absent red light reflex in right eye" in a 6-month-old: an abnormal red reflex means leukocoria until proven otherwise, with retinoblastoma and congenital cataract as the key causes. Combined with "right esotropia since birth" (strabismus can be the first sign of a poorly seeing eye), this requires prompt referral to ophthalmology for a dilated eye examination. The negative cover test does not change this, since the red reflex finding alone mandates referral.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance is only for pseudostrabismus with a normal, symmetric red reflex and corneal light reflex; an absent red reflex is never normal and may be a malignancy.
key_concept:
Abnormal red reflex in an infant means urgent ophthalmology referral.
  • Leukocoria causes: retinoblastoma, congenital cataract
  • Strabismus may be the presenting sign of retinoblastoma
  • Referral is immediate, not a routine appointment; imaging comes after the dilated exam
  • Untreated strabismus or media opacity leads to amblyopia
exam_pearl: Strabismus plus an absent or white red reflex is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise: refer now, never reassure.

stem: Middle aged man came with metal objects lodged in his eye. What to do next?
highlight_terms_source: metal objects lodged in his eye
why_right: The clue is a metal object lodged in the eye: an embedded or possibly penetrating foreign body is beyond safe removal in a general setting. The correct next step is to leave it in place, protect the eye with a rigid shield (no pressure) and refer urgently to ophthalmology for slit lamp assessment, imaging for retained intraocular metal and removal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Removal and irrigation suit a superficial, loose foreign body or a chemical splash; pulling out a lodged metal object can worsen a penetrating injury and cause extrusion of ocular contents.
C. Antibiotics with clinic follow up fit a simple corneal abrasion after a superficial foreign body has been removed, not an object still embedded in the eye.
D. A pressure patch is avoided in suspected penetrating injury because pressure on the globe can expel contents; a rigid shield is used only as a bridge to referral, not as the management.
key_concept:
Ocular foreign body: superficial and loose = remove/irrigate; embedded or suspected penetrating = do not remove, shield, refer.
  • Superficial FB: topical anaesthetic, irrigate or lift off, then treat as abrasion
  • Embedded or high velocity metal (hammering, grinding): suspect intraocular FB
  • Suspected globe injury: rigid shield, no pressure, no drops, urgent ophthalmology
  • Metal FB imaging: CT orbit (MRI contraindicated)
  • Rust ring after metal FB: removed by ophthalmology
exam_pearl: A lodged or high velocity metal fragment means possible open globe: shield and refer, never pull it out or apply a pressure patch.

stem: A hypertensive man presents with a bright red spot in the eye. No pain, no vision change, no infection signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bright red spot in the eye
why_right: A bright red, well demarcated patch on the white of the eye with no pain, no visual change and no discharge is the classic subconjunctival hemorrhage. Hypertension is a recognised risk factor (fragile conjunctival vessels), along with straining, coughing, trauma and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use. It is benign and resolves on its own over about 2 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conjunctivitis gives diffuse redness with discharge, grittiness or itch, usually bilateral; here there are no infection signs and the redness is a solid spot.
B. Scleritis causes severe, boring pain (often waking the patient), tenderness and a deep violaceous hue, and can threaten vision; this patient has no pain.
C. Episcleritis gives sectoral pinkish redness of dilated vessels with mild discomfort; it is engorged vessels, not a flat sheet of blood obscuring the sclera.
key_concept:
Painless red eye with a flat bright red patch, normal vision, no discharge = subconjunctival hemorrhage.
  • Risks: hypertension, Valsalva/cough, trauma, anticoagulants or antiplatelets, bleeding disorders
  • Management: reassure, check BP; resolves over about 2 weeks
  • Recurrent: check BP, INR or bleeding screen
  • Traumatic with no posterior limit: think orbital or skull base fracture
exam_pearl: Pain or reduced vision with a red eye points away from subconjunctival hemorrhage toward scleritis, keratitis, uveitis or glaucoma.

stem: 2 month old; his mother mentioned she noticed his right eye goes inward while feeding, she's concerned. What's the most initial management? (Esotropia)
why_right: The clues are age 2 months and an eye that turns inward only while feeding, i.e. intermittent. Binocular control is still immature in the first few months, so intermittent misalignment is normal and the initial management is to reassure the mother and re-examine at follow up.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
B. Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.
key_concept:
Infant eye alignment: intermittent misalignment in the first months is normal; constant or persistent deviation is not.
  • Under about 4 months, intermittent, normal red reflex: reassure and recheck
  • Constant deviation at any age: refer
  • Any deviation persisting after about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia risk)
  • Abnormal or absent red reflex: urgent referral (retinoblastoma, cataract)
  • Symmetric corneal light reflex with apparent squint: pseudostrabismus (epicanthal folds)
exam_pearl: Same infant with a constant inward turn, or still deviating after about 4 to 6 months, needs referral, not reassurance.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0412).

stem: Case of child with leukocoria with well-demarcated retinal lesions and calcifications. Ask about diagnosis:
why_right: Leukocoria in a young child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise, and the decisive clue here is calcification within a retinal mass. Intralesional calcification is the hallmark of retinoblastoma on fundoscopy and ultrasound and is what separates it from its mimics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ocular toxocariasis gives a granuloma with vitreous inflammation in an older child with puppy contact; calcification is not its typical feature.
C. Coats disease (usually a young boy, unilateral) gives telangiectatic vessels with yellow subretinal exudate and exudative detachment, typically without calcification.
D. Congenital rubella causes cataract (absent red reflex) with microcephaly, PDA and deafness, not a calcified retinal mass.
key_concept:
Leukocoria + retinal mass with calcification = retinoblastoma.
  • Common leukocoria causes: retinoblastoma, congenital cataract
  • Mimics: Coats disease (exudates), toxocariasis (granuloma), persistent fetal vasculature, ROP
  • Next step for any leukocoria: urgent ophthalmology, dilated exam
  • Retinoblastoma: RB1 gene; hereditary forms are bilateral and present earlier
exam_pearl: Calcification on fundoscopy or ultrasound swings the leukocoria differential to retinoblastoma; exudates without calcium suggest Coats.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Printed as 256 between 355 and 357 (likely a typo for 356). Restatement: 1-year-old infant with leukocoria, fundoscopy shows stable non-progressive retinal calcifications, no family history of eye disease; options A-Toxocariasis, B-Coat's disease, C-Retinoblastoma (highlighted).

stem: A 2 month old his mother mentioned noticed his right eye goes inward while feeding, she's concerned, what's the most initial management? I Am Not Sure If Same Recall Or Not, But It Had Normal Red Reflex & Corneal Reflex
why_right: A 2 month old whose eye goes inward while feeding (intermittent) with a normal red reflex and normal corneal light reflex has no sign of true strabismus or intraocular pathology. Intermittent misalignment is normal at this age, so the initial management is to reassure and recheck.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
B. Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.
key_concept:
Infant eye alignment: intermittent misalignment in the first months is normal; constant or persistent deviation is not.
  • Under about 4 months, intermittent, normal red reflex: reassure and recheck
  • Constant deviation at any age: refer
  • Any deviation persisting after about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia risk)
  • Abnormal or absent red reflex: urgent referral (retinoblastoma, cataract)
  • Symmetric corneal light reflex with apparent squint: pseudostrabismus (epicanthal folds)
exam_pearl: An abnormal red reflex flips this to urgent ophthalmology referral; an asymmetric corneal light reflex or constant deviation also needs referral.

stem: A 6 month old pediatric came with convergence and esotropia and during exam Intact corneal light reflex The parents are concerned what should you do?
why_right: The decisive clue is an intact (symmetric) corneal light reflex. The Hirschberg test is the screening test for strabismus: if the reflexes are centred and symmetric the eyes are truly aligned, and the apparent inward turning is pseudoesotropia, usually from a broad nasal bridge and epicanthal folds. The parents should be reassured.
why_wrong_block: B. Referral is right when the corneal light reflex is displaced (temporally in the deviated eye in esotropia), the cover test shows movement, the deviation is constant, or the red reflex is abnormal.
key_concept:
Apparent squint + symmetric corneal light reflex = pseudostrabismus: reassure.
  • Hirschberg: reflex centred and symmetric = aligned
  • Esotropia: reflex displaced temporally in the deviated eye
  • Exotropia: reflex displaced nasally
  • True strabismus persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months: refer (amblyopia)
exam_pearl: The parents' concern does not change management; the corneal light reflex does. Asymmetric reflex = refer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Infant <6 months with intermittent esotropia + normal corneal reflex: normal, reassure. Persistent/constant deviation after 6 months: refer.

stem: A Hypertensive man On Aspirin came with a bright red spot in his eye, he denied pain, visual changes, no signs of infection, what's the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bright red spot in his eye
why_right: A hypertensive man on aspirin with a bright red spot, no pain, no visual change and no infection signs has a subconjunctival hemorrhage. Both hypertension and antiplatelet therapy predispose to rupture of small conjunctival vessels; the condition is benign and resolves without treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conjunctivitis gives diffuse injection with discharge and irritation; there are no infection signs and the redness is a localised patch.
B. Scleritis is severely painful and tender with a deep violet hue, often linked to autoimmune disease; this eye is painless.
C. Episcleritis shows sectoral engorged vessels with mild discomfort, not a flat sheet of extravasated blood.
key_concept:
Painless bright red patch, normal vision, no discharge = subconjunctival hemorrhage.
  • Risks: hypertension, aspirin or anticoagulants, Valsalva, trauma
  • Management: reassure, check BP; no need to stop aspirin for this alone
  • On warfarin or recurrent: check INR or bleeding screen
exam_pearl: Add pain, photophobia or reduced vision and it is no longer a subconjunctival hemorrhage question.

stem: A pediatric patient with white eye reflex. What to order to confirm diagnosis
why_right: A child with leukocoria is suspected of retinoblastoma. This recall's key is MRI because it is the imaging of choice to characterise the tumour and assess optic nerve, orbital and intracranial extension without exposing the child to radiation, which matters because hereditary RB1 carriers are at risk of radiation induced second cancers.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT shows calcification well but is avoided in suspected retinoblastoma because ionising radiation raises second cancer risk in RB1 carriers.
C. Ocular ultrasound (B scan) is the quick bedside test that demonstrates an intraocular mass with calcification; it is not the keyed answer here but is often used first.
D. Plain X ray has no role in evaluating an intraocular mass.
key_concept:
Leukocoria workup: urgent ophthalmology, dilated fundus exam under anaesthesia, then imaging without radiation.
  • Ultrasound B scan: confirms intraocular mass and calcification
  • MRI orbits and brain: extent, optic nerve invasion, pineal lesion
  • CT: avoided (radiation, second cancers in RB1 carriers)
  • Biopsy: not done (risk of tumour seeding)
exam_pearl: CT is the trap: it shows calcium best but is avoided in retinoblastoma because of radiation.

stem: A patient presents after a small wooden object entered his eye. He complains of severe eye pain, inability to open the eye, and photophobia. An eye examination was performed using fluorescein staining, which showed an epithelial injury or tear something like that What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small wooden object entered his eye
why_right: Acute onset after a small object entered the eye, with severe pain, inability to open the eye and photophobia, and fluorescein uptake showing an epithelial defect is a corneal abrasion. Fluorescein stains areas where the corneal epithelium is missing, and a linear defect fits a scratch from the foreign body.
why_wrong_block:
A. A corneal ulcer (infective keratitis) develops over days, often in contact lens wearers, and shows a white infiltrate or opacity with a staining defect; this is an immediate traumatic defect.
C. Subconjunctival hemorrhage is painless with a bright red patch and no fluorescein uptake.
D. Acute conjunctivitis gives redness with discharge and grittiness, usually without severe pain or a staining epithelial defect.
key_concept:
Trauma + pain + photophobia + fluorescein uptake = corneal abrasion.
  • Evert lids to look for a retained foreign body (vertical linear abrasions)
  • Treat: topical antibiotic, analgesia; no steroid drops
  • Do not give topical anaesthetic to take home
  • Vegetable matter or contact lens: watch for infective keratitis
  • Opacity or infiltrate = ulcer, refer
exam_pearl: A white infiltrate over the staining area, or symptoms evolving over days, turns an abrasion into a corneal ulcer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: cutting woods, felt something in eye, tearing, photosensitivity, cannot close the eye, normal visual acuity, fluorescein shows linear epithelial lesion; options corneal abrasion (highlighted) / corneal ulcer.

stem: A well circumscribed red swelling under the conjunctiva
key_concept:
Red eye nodule: decide by pain, colour and blanching.
  • Episcleritis: mild or no pain, bright red, mobile, blanches with phenylephrine, self limiting
  • Scleritis: severe boring pain, violaceous, tender, non blanching, vision threatening
  • Scleritis: look for RA, vasculitis; needs urgent ophthalmology and systemic therapy
  • Flat bright red patch with no swelling: subconjunctival hemorrhage
exam_pearl: Severe pain is the single feature that moves a localised red eye from episcleritis to scleritis.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic for a check-up. When performing a cover test, the child's deft eye moves laterally when the right eye is covered. The family hesitate to start treatment Which of the following is the most serious complication?
highlight_terms_source: moves laterally when the right eye is covered
why_right: On the cover test, the uncovered left eye moving to take up fixation when the right is covered means the left eye was deviated at rest: a manifest squint in a 4-year-old. Because the family "hesitate to start treatment", the brain keeps suppressing the image from the deviated eye, and this leads to amblyopia, a permanent loss of vision if not treated within the visual development window. That irreversible vision loss is why amblyopia is the most serious complication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Strabismus is the condition already present (the cover test shows it), not its complication.
B. Nystagmus is a separate oscillation disorder (congenital, or from early severe visual loss or neurological disease); it is not the expected result of untreated squint.
D. Leukocoria is a white pupillary reflex from retinoblastoma or cataract; it can be a CAUSE of squint, not a consequence of untreated squint.
key_concept:
Untreated childhood squint → suppression of the deviated eye → amblyopia (lazy eye).
  • Cover test: the uncovered eye moving to fixate = manifest squint (tropia)
  • Eye moves outward to fixate = it was turned in (esotropia); moves inward = exotropia
  • Screening at any age: corneal light reflex (Hirschberg) and red reflex
  • Treatment: correct refractive error (glasses), patching or atropine penalization of the good eye, surgery for alignment
  • Results are best when treated early in childhood
exam_pearl: Any squint in a child needs ophthalmology review; leukocoria with squint means exclude retinoblastoma first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 'Q:' version: 5 years old girl with convergent squint for the last two years, mother hesitated to start treatment; complication? Cataract / amblyopia ✅ / Optic neuritis / Retinal detachment.

stem: Pedia (7 months maybe) Constant squint/converge
why_right: Intermittent misalignment can be normal in the first few months of life, but a CONSTANT squint ("constant ... converge") at about 7 months is never physiological. It needs referral to ophthalmology to exclude an organic cause (refractive error, cataract, retinoblastoma) and to prevent amblyopia.
why_wrong_block: A. Observation is only acceptable for intermittent deviation in early infancy (roughly the first 4 months); waiting until 24 months with a constant squint risks amblyopia and a missed tumour or cataract.
key_concept:
Squint in infants: intermittent and early = can observe; constant or persisting = refer.
  • Constant squint at any age → ophthalmology referral
  • Any squint persisting beyond early infancy → referral
  • Always check the red reflex: leukocoria with squint suggests retinoblastoma or cataract
  • Untreated squint → amblyopia
exam_pearl: The word "constant" flips the answer from observe to refer, whatever the age.

stem: 2 y.o evaluated for squint, white pupil instead of red reflex, how to diagnose?
highlight_terms_source: white pupil instead of red reflex
why_right: A 2-year-old with squint and "white pupil instead of red reflex" (leukocoria) has retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Among the imaging options, MRI is preferred because it defines intraocular extent and optic nerve and intracranial spread without radiation, which matters since hereditary retinoblastoma carries a high risk of radiation-induced second cancers. Clinical diagnosis itself is by dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia by an ophthalmologist.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT shows the characteristic calcification but is avoided because of radiation exposure in a child who may carry an RB1 germline mutation.
C. Ocular ultrasound is a useful bedside test showing a calcified intraocular mass, but it cannot assess optic nerve or intracranial extension; it would be the answer if the question asked for the first bedside imaging.
D. Plain X-ray gives no useful detail of an intraocular mass and adds radiation.
key_concept:
Leukocoria + squint in a young child = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
  • Next step: urgent ophthalmology referral, dilated fundus exam under anaesthesia
  • Imaging of choice for extent: MRI orbits and brain
  • Ultrasound: shows calcification, no radiation
  • Avoid CT: radiation, second malignancy risk (RB1)
  • Other leukocoria cause: congenital cataract
exam_pearl: If "refer to ophthalmology" or "fundoscopy under anaesthesia" is offered, that beats any imaging choice.

stem: A 6-year-old child is complaining that he cannot see the board in his classroom. He was diagnosed with Hypermetropia. Which of the following is the best next step?
OptD: Cover one eye / Contact lenses / Artificial tears
why_right: The card states the child "was diagnosed with Hypermetropia". In hypermetropia the eye is too short, so light focuses behind the retina; a convex (plus) lens converges light to bring the focus onto the retina. Symptomatic hypermetropia in a school-age child is corrected with convex spectacles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits mild asymptomatic hypermetropia in young children; this child is symptomatic, so correction is needed.
B. Concave (minus) lenses diverge light and correct myopia, where the image focuses in front of the retina.
D. Patching treats amblyopia (after refractive correction), contact lenses are not first line in a young child, and artificial tears treat dry eye.
key_concept:
Lens rule: Hypermetropia = convex (plus); Myopia = concave (minus).
  • Myopia: eye too long, blurred DISTANCE vision (cannot see the board)
  • Hypermetropia: eye too short, near vision worse, eye strain, risk of convergent squint and amblyopia
  • Astigmatism: cylindrical lens
  • Presbyopia: convex reading glasses
exam_pearl: "Cannot see the board" usually means myopia; follow the diagnosis stated in the stem to pick the lens.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version: 'Preschool child with hypermetropia. What you will do?' A. Concave glasses B. Convex glasses C. Covered one eye; Answer: B. 'Q:' fuller version Answer: Convex lenses.

stem: Patient presented to the clinic with eye redness on examination there is bilateral redness and wet discharge. Asking about next step in management?
OptD: Something about observe and wet wipes or eye drops ( can’t remember exactly)
key_concept:
Bilateral red eye with discharge and no red flags = conjunctivitis, usually self-limiting.
  • Watery + URTI + preauricular node: viral, supportive care
  • Purulent, lids stuck in morning: bacterial, hygiene ± topical antibiotic
  • Itch + watery + atopy: allergic, antihistamine or mast cell stabiliser drops
  • Hyperacute copious pus: gonococcal, systemic antibiotic, urgent referral
  • Red flags (pain, photophobia, reduced vision, unequal pupil): refer
exam_pearl: Topical steroid for an undiagnosed red eye is the classic wrong move.

stem: Treatment of chalazion:
why_right: A chalazion is a sterile, painless granulomatous lump from a blocked meibomian gland, not an infection. First-line treatment is warm compresses with lid massage several times a day, and most resolve within weeks to months.
why_wrong_block: A. Antibiotics do not help a sterile granuloma; they are reserved for a secondarily infected lesion or associated preseptal cellulitis.
key_concept:
Chalazion = painless, sterile, meibomian gland lump; hordeolum (stye) = painful acute infection.
  • Chalazion first line: warm compress and lid massage
  • Persistent chalazion: incision and curettage or intralesional steroid
  • Recurrent chalazion in the same site in an older adult: biopsy to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma
  • Stye: also warm compress; antibiotics only if spreading infection
exam_pearl: Recurrent chalazion at the same spot in an elderly patient = biopsy, not more compresses.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of fever and painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest. His physical examination reveals a skin eruption consisting of maculopapular lesions and vesicles with some skin crusting over the left side of his chest. His systemic examinations are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to confirm the diagnosis?
OptC: Swab from skin lesion for culture
highlight_terms_source: painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest
maculopapular lesions and vesicles with some skin crusting
why_right: A "painful skin eruption over the left side of his chest" with "maculopapular lesions and vesicles" and "crusting" is a unilateral dermatomal rash, the textbook picture of herpes zoster (shingles). Shingles is a clinical diagnosis, so in a typical presentation in a systemically well patient no investigation is needed to confirm it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin biopsy is invasive and unnecessary for a typical dermatomal zoster rash; it is used for atypical lesions or suspected malignancy.
B. Zoster is VZV reactivation; blood cultures detect bacteria and have no role in a systemically well patient.
C. Viral culture is slow and insensitive and not required here; lesion swab for PCR is reserved for atypical or disseminated cases or immunocompromised patients.
key_concept:
Herpes zoster: dermatomal, unilateral, painful vesicular rash = clinical diagnosis.
  • Prodrome: pain or burning before the rash
  • Does not cross the midline
  • Typical case: no tests
  • Atypical or immunocompromised: vesicle swab PCR
  • Treat with oral antiviral (acyclovir, valacyclovir) early
exam_pearl: Unilateral band-like vesicular rash that stops at the midline = shingles; the answer is "no investigation" unless the picture is atypical.

stem: A child with atopic dermatitis (eczema) has been treated with topical corticosteroids and emollients with minimal improvement. What is the best next step in management?
OptC: Start topical calcineurin inhibitors (EG: tacrolimus, pimecrolimus)
highlight_terms_source: topical corticosteroids and emollients with minimal improvement
why_right: The child has eczema with "minimal improvement" on topical corticosteroids and emollients. The next step on the eczema ladder is a steroid-sparing topical agent, a topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus), which controls inflammation without skin atrophy and is useful on the face and flexures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Elimination diets are not recommended routinely; they are used only when a specific food allergy is proven or strongly suspected to trigger flares.
B. Systemic corticosteroids cause rebound flares and long-term adverse effects in children; they are avoided except for short courses in severe flares under specialist care.
key_concept:
Eczema ladder: emollients + trigger avoidance → topical steroid → topical calcineurin inhibitor → phototherapy or systemic agents (specialist).
  • Check adherence and steroid phobia before escalating
  • Calcineurin inhibitors: steroid sparing, no skin atrophy, good for face and flexures
  • Infected eczema: treat the infection
  • Refractory severe disease: refer to dermatology
exam_pearl: If an option asks about compliance or parental concerns, that comes before escalating therapy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot; option C highlighted in pink; compiler line: 'Answer: C, Calcineurin Inhibitors'.

stem: male patient presented to the clinic worried regarding the possibility of melanoma, given a family history of melanoma (his father)The patient has multiple benign nevi
why_right: A patient with "multiple" nevi plus a first-degree relative (his father) with melanoma has two major melanoma risk factors. He should be referred to a dermatologist for a full skin examination, baseline mapping and regular surveillance, and taught self-examination and sun protection.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance alone ignores his raised risk; it fits a low-risk patient with few typical nevi and no family history.
key_concept:
Melanoma risk: many nevi (or atypical nevi), family history, fair skin, sunburn history, immunosuppression, previous melanoma.
  • High risk → dermatology surveillance (full skin exam, ± photography or dermoscopy)
  • Suspicious lesion (ABCDE change) → excisional biopsy with narrow margins
  • Education: sun protection and monthly self-examination
exam_pearl: A changing or ABCDE-positive mole changes the answer from referral for surveillance to excisional biopsy.

stem: Patient presents with a warm, erythematous swelling of the thigh with indistinct borders, accompanied by lymphangitis, and regional lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A "warm, erythematous swelling" with "indistinct borders" is the classic description of cellulitis, an infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. Accompanying lymphangitis (red streaks) and regional lymphadenopathy show spread along lymphatics, which fits streptococcal cellulitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Necrotizing fasciitis shows pain out of proportion to findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis; none are described here.
B. Folliculitis gives small pustules centred on hair follicles, not a diffuse warm swelling with lymphangitis.
D. Impetigo is a superficial epidermal infection with honey-coloured crusts, typically on the face of children.
key_concept:
Skin infection depth: impetigo (epidermis) → erysipelas (upper dermis, SHARP raised border) → cellulitis (deep dermis/subcutis, INDISTINCT border) → necrotizing fasciitis (fascia).
  • Cellulitis: oral anti-staphylococcal/streptococcal antibiotic; IV if systemic features
  • Fluctuant collection = abscess → drainage
  • Pain out of proportion, crepitus, toxicity → necrotizing fasciitis → urgent surgical debridement
exam_pearl: Sharp, raised, well-demarcated border flips the diagnosis to erysipelas.

stem: Child with dry patches in face, scalp and extensor surfaces. Sometimes his cheeks are cracked and red and weepy
highlight_terms_source: dry patches in face, scalp and extensor surfaces
cheeks are cracked and red and weepy
why_right: A child with dry patches on the face, scalp and extensor surfaces has the classic infant and toddler distribution of atopic eczema. Red, cracked, weepy cheeks describe acute eczema with exudation. Dry skin plus this age specific distribution makes atopic dermatitis the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Idiopathic urticaria: transient itchy wheals that come and go within 24 hours and leave normal skin; it does not cause dry, cracked, weeping patches in a fixed distribution.
C. Drug induced dermatitis: needs a new drug exposure and usually gives an acute widespread eruption; right when a rash follows a recently started medication.
D. Unrecalled option: no content to judge; the distribution and dry, weepy skin already point to atopic dermatitis.
key_concept:
Atopic eczema: dry, intensely itchy skin with a distribution that changes with age.
  • Under 6 months: face, head and scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae)
  • Over 12 years: flexures and perioral region
  • Treatment: emollients, non soap cleansers, topical corticosteroids as the cornerstone
  • Honey colored crusts on eczema: secondary impetigo
exam_pearl: Extensor surfaces plus cheeks means a young child's eczema; flexures mean an older child.

stem: A patient notices one or more sharply marginated, scaling, and red plaques predominantly involving only the vulva. Psoriasis is suspected. Which of the following is required for a definitive diagnosis of psoriasis?
highlight_terms_source: sharply marginated, scaling, and red plaques
why_right: The lead in asks what is required for a definitive diagnosis, not how psoriasis is usually diagnosed. Histology (acanthosis, parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, neutrophil microabscesses) is the only option that confirms it. On the vulva, plaques often lose their typical scale and mimic lichen simplex, lichen sclerosus, candidiasis or VIN, so biopsy is the confirmatory test.
why_wrong_block:
B. Staining using iodine: Lugol iodine (Schiller test) is used on the cervix and vagina to outline abnormal epithelium; it does not diagnose psoriasis.
C. Clinical diagnosis is sufficient: true for typical psoriasis in everyday practice, but the question asks for a definitive diagnosis, which needs histology; right when the lead in is 'how is it usually diagnosed'.
D. Potassium hydroxide skin scraping: confirms fungal infection (hyphae or yeast) such as tinea cruris or candidiasis; useful to exclude a mimic, not to prove psoriasis.
key_concept:
'Definitive' or 'confirm' in the lead in points to histology, even for diseases usually diagnosed clinically.
  • Typical psoriasis: clinical diagnosis in practice
  • Definitive diagnosis: skin biopsy
  • KOH scraping: fungal infection
  • Lugol iodine: cervix and vagina screening aid
  • Vulvar psoriasis: often non scaly, well demarcated red plaques
exam_pearl: Read the verb: 'usually diagnosed' is clinical, 'definitive diagnosis' is biopsy.

stem: A 25 years old woman presents with sever acne following with a dermatologist who prescribed her ISOTRETINOIN and advised her not to get pregnant. She asks when she can try to get pregnant, what is the most appropriate (counseling?) regarding her pregnancy?
OptA: The medication is safe to take during pregnancy
OptB: She can try to get pregnant after she finishes the treatment
OptC: Stop and try to get pregnant immediately
OptD: She can try to get pregnant after 3 months of stoping the medication
highlight_terms_source: when she can try to get pregnant
why_right: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, so the counseling must include a drug free waiting period after the last dose before trying to conceive. Option D is the only choice that builds in a washout after stopping the medication; every other option allows pregnancy on the drug or with no interval. This recall's key is the 3 month interval.
why_wrong_block:
A. The medication is safe to take during pregnancy: false; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations and is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
B. She can try to get pregnant after she finishes the treatment: omits the required drug free interval after the last dose, so conception could occur while the drug is still present.
C. Stop and try to get pregnant immediately: no washout period at all; conception must wait after the last dose.
key_concept:
Isotretinoin: teratogen requiring pregnancy prevention before, during and after treatment.
  • Pregnancy test before starting and during treatment
  • Effective contraception during therapy
  • Drug free wait after the last dose before conception (this recall keys 3 months)
  • Teratogenic effects: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS defects
  • Acitretin is the retinoid with a much longer post treatment interval (years)
  • Pregnancy on isotretinoin: stop the drug and refer for counseling
exam_pearl: Never 'immediately' or 'once treatment ends': isotretinoin counseling always includes a drug free wait after the last dose.

stem: A female patient on isotretinoin for Acne. wishes to conceive. What should the physician tell her about the appropriate time?
OptA: She can conceive as soon as she stops the isotretinoin
OptB: She can conceive while taking isotretinoin
OptC: She can conceive after 3 months off of isotretinoin
OptD: She can conceive after 1 month of stopping isotretinoin
why_right: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic but has a short half life, so conception should wait until it has cleared. Current pregnancy prevention guidance asks women to avoid pregnancy for 1 month after stopping, which makes D the correct counseling on the appropriate time to conceive.
why_wrong_block:
A. She can conceive as soon as she stops the isotretinoin: no washout; conception must wait 1 month after the last dose.
B. She can conceive while taking isotretinoin: absolutely contraindicated; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations.
C. She can conceive after 3 months off isotretinoin: overly long for isotretinoin; long post treatment intervals apply to acitretin, not isotretinoin.
key_concept:
Isotretinoin: avoid pregnancy during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose.
  • Negative pregnancy test before starting and monthly during treatment
  • Effective contraception during therapy and for 1 month after
  • Teratogenic effects: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS defects
  • Acitretin: much longer post treatment avoidance (years)
exam_pearl: Isotretinoin is 1 month; do not confuse it with acitretin's years long wait.

stem: A 19-year-old woman 23-week pregnant primigravida presents with a complaint of irregular brownish patches of varying sizes on face and neck (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 23 week primigravida with irregular brownish patches on the face and neck has hormone driven facial hyperpigmentation of pregnancy. When this pattern appears in pregnancy it is called chloasma (the 'mask of pregnancy'), which is the term this recall keys. It is caused by estrogen and progesterone stimulating melanocytes and is worsened by sun exposure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Melasma: the same pigmentary process (chloasma is melasma occurring in pregnancy); the recall prefers the pregnancy specific term, while melasma fits a non pregnant woman, for example on oral contraceptives.
C. Tinea nigra: a painless brown to black macule, usually single, on the palms or soles; it does not cause symmetric facial patches.
D. Lichen planus: itchy, purple, polygonal, flat topped papules with Wickham striae on wrists, shins and oral mucosa; not brown facial patches.
key_concept:
Brown facial patches in pregnancy = chloasma (melasma of pregnancy).
  • Sites: cheeks, forehead, upper lip, nose
  • Cause: estrogen and progesterone stimulating melanocytes; worse with sun
  • Often fades after delivery; may persist
  • Management: sun protection and reassurance in pregnancy
  • Other pregnancy pigment changes: linea nigra, darkened areolae
exam_pearl: Same lesion, two names: in pregnancy the exam wants chloasma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'B. Chloasma (MG)'. Image referenced but not shown on page.

stem: A man presents with small papules on his face after shaving. (No pain, tenderness, erythema, or purulent discharge was mentioned.) What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small papules on his face after shaving
key_concept:
Size and depth decide: superficial follicular papules or pustules = folliculitis; deep tender nodule = furuncle; several merged furuncles = carbuncle.
  • Folliculitis: small perifollicular papules or pustules, sites of shaving, sweat and abrasion
  • Furuncle (boil): tender nodule around one follicle, drain if fluctuant
  • Carbuncle: several adjacent follicles, plaque with multiple pus points, classically the nape of the neck
  • Pseudofolliculitis barbae: ingrown beard hairs after close shaving, small papules in the beard area
exam_pearl: Many small follicular papules = folliculitis; one big painful nodule = furuncle.
